## Decision: Utilize Amazon S3 as the primary storage solution for digital object bitstreams in DOS, including PDFs and JPEGs.

Rationale: Amazon S3 is selected as the storage backend for digital object bitstreams due to its proven reliability, scalability, and integration with existing DLS infrastructure. S3 provides durable, highly available object storage with built-in redundancy, ensuring long-term preservation and accessibility of digital assets. Its support for versioning, encryption (at rest and in transit), and access control policies aligns with the security and compliance requirements for digital collections. Leveraging S3 also eliminates the need for managing physical storage hardware or local file systems, reducing operational overhead. Given that S3 is already in use across multiple DLS projects, the team benefits from shared expertise, standardized configurations, and established operational procedures. This decision ensures consistency, minimizes technical debt, and enables future scalability as the volume of digital objects grows. All bitstream uploads, retrievals, and metadata associations will be managed through secure, programmatic interfaces using AWS SDKs, with access governed by role-based permissions. The use of S3 also facilitates integration with downstream services such as digital preservation systems, search indexes, and delivery mechanisms. This approach supports both current needs and future extensibility, including potential support for additional file formats.

## Decision

Decompose the CiviCRM monolithic system by extracting core contact management and subscription handling functionality into a dedicated, independently deployable microservice. This new service will be built using modern, well-documented technologies with strong developer tooling and in-house expertise (e.g., Node.js/TypeScript, PostgreSQL, REST/GraphQL APIs). The microservice will expose a clean, versioned API for managing contacts, subscriptions, and related metadata, replacing direct CiviCRM database access. Existing CiviCRM functionality not required by the new service will be deprecated and eventually phased out. All integrations with other systems (e.g., publishing workflows, email campaigns) will be reconfigured to interact exclusively with the new microservice via its API. The migration will be executed incrementally using a dual-write pattern during the transition, ensuring data consistency. This approach eliminates dependency on external consultants for core functionality, enables faster iteration, improves testability and observability, and aligns with eLife’s long-term goal of a modular, maintainable architecture. The decision prioritizes sustainability, developer velocity, and architectural clarity over short-term convenience of maintaining the legacy system.

## Decision

Files shall be formatted automatically using a standardized code formatter integrated into the development workflow. The formatter will be configured to enforce consistent style across the codebase, including indentation, spacing, naming conventions, and syntax formatting. Formatting will be applied as part of the pre-commit hook and enforced via CI/CD pipelines to prevent unformatted code from being merged. This decision ensures uniform code quality, reduces friction in code reviews, and eliminates subjective debates over formatting style. The chosen formatter will be Prettier for JavaScript/TypeScript and Black for Python, with configuration files committed to the repository to ensure consistency across all environments. Developers are not permitted to disable or bypass formatting, and any deviations will be rejected during CI validation. This approach prioritizes maintainability, readability, and team productivity by eliminating formatting as a point of contention.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, consistent response envelope pattern across all server-side endpoints within the klokwrk-project, regardless of the underlying transport protocol (e.g., HTTP, gRPC, messaging). The response envelope shall follow a fixed structure with two primary components: a `metadata` object and a `payload` object. The `metadata` object will contain standardized fields such as `requestId`, `timestamp`, `correlationId`, `status` (e.g., success, error, warning), `code` (a domain-specific error code), `message` (a human-readable description), and optional `details` for extended diagnostic information. The `payload` object will carry the domain-specific data for successful responses or be null/absent for errors. This envelope is applied uniformly across all endpoints and transport layers, ensuring consistent handling of both success and failure responses. The format shall be JSON for RESTful APIs and compatible with protocol-specific serialization (e.g., Protobuf for gRPC) via a common interface. Client-side logic will be built around this envelope, enabling generic processing, logging, monitoring, and error handling without dependency on endpoint-specific response shapes. This decision enables decoupling of metadata from protocol-specific mechanisms (e.g., HTTP status codes, headers), reduces implementation fragmentation, and improves observability, maintainability, and interoperability across the system.

## Decision: Adopt React as the primary front-end framework for the application.

React is selected as the foundational framework due to its proven scalability, performance, and extensive ecosystem. Its component-based architecture enables modular, reusable, and maintainable code, which is critical for long-term development and team collaboration. React’s virtual DOM efficiently minimizes direct manipulation of the actual DOM, resulting in high rendering performance even with dynamic and complex user interfaces. The framework’s strong support for server-side rendering (via Next.js) and static site generation enhances SEO and initial load performance, aligning with modern web standards. React’s vast ecosystem—including tools like Redux for state management, React Router for navigation, and ESLint/Prettier for code quality—ensures rapid development with consistent best practices. Additionally, React’s strong community, extensive documentation, and widespread industry adoption guarantee long-term sustainability, talent availability, and robust third-party library support. The framework’s compatibility with modern build tools (Webpack, Vite) and support for TypeScript further enhance type safety, developer experience, and performance optimization. While alternatives like Vue or Angular exist, React’s balance of flexibility, performance, and ecosystem maturity makes it the optimal choice for building a scalable, performant, and efficient front-end solution.

## Decision

Adopt a blue-green deployment strategy using container orchestration via Kubernetes, with a focus on zero-downtime updates and automated rollouts. Replace the current systemd-based deployment with a Kubernetes-managed deployment that runs cljdoc as a containerized application. Each release will be deployed as a new versioned Kubernetes Deployment, with a corresponding Service routing traffic to the active version. A new deployment will be brought online in parallel with the existing one, and once health checks pass, the load balancer (via the Service) will gradually shift traffic to the new version using a rolling update strategy. The old version will remain available until the new version is verified and stable, at which point the old deployment will be scaled down and terminated. This approach eliminates downtime during updates, enables safe canary releases, and provides a declarative, repeatable, and version-controlled deployment process. The existing S3-based artifact delivery will be retained, but the deployment pipeline will now use Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts to manage the application lifecycle. This shift reduces reliance on fragile bash scripts, improves reliability, and enables Continuous Deployment by allowing automated, safe, and incremental rollouts without manual intervention or risk of service disruption.

## Decision: Integrate Static Application Security Testing (SAST) and Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) tools into the CI/CD pipeline with automated vulnerability scanning and blocking on critical findings.

We will implement SAST and DAST tools—such as SonarQube, Snyk, or Checkmarx for SAST, and OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite for DAST—as mandatory stages within the CI/CD pipeline. SAST will analyze source code during build phases to detect insecure coding practices, vulnerabilities like SQL injection, XSS, and insecure deserialization, while DAST will perform runtime testing on deployed artifacts in staging environments to identify exploitable vulnerabilities in the running application. Scans will be triggered automatically on every pull request and merge to main, with results reported in real time to developers. The pipeline will enforce a security gate: any critical or high-severity vulnerability detected will block the build or deployment, requiring remediation before proceeding. Results will be enriched with contextual guidance, including CWE references, remediation steps, and code examples. Security findings will be tracked in a centralized dashboard accessible to development, security, and DevOps teams, enabling auditability and trend analysis. To reduce false positives and improve developer adoption, we will configure scan rules based on our technology stack and business risk profile, with periodic tuning and feedback loops. This approach ensures early detection of vulnerabilities, shifts security left in the development lifecycle, and enforces a consistent, automated security posture across all code changes prior to production.

## Decision: Implement a unified refund handling abstraction layer within Shopware's core, enabling all payment extensions to leverage a consistent, standardized refund interface.

To address the lack of unified refund handling across Shopware payment extensions, a dedicated refund handling abstraction layer will be introduced at the core level. This layer will define a standardized interface for initiating, processing, and tracking refunds, decoupling the logic from individual payment provider implementations. The abstraction will support common refund operations—partial and full refunds, refund reasons, refund tracking, and status synchronization—while allowing extension-specific implementations to be registered and invoked through a common API.

The core refund handler will be designed as a service with dependency injection, allowing payment extensions to register their refund strategies via event subscribers or service providers. Each extension will implement a `RefundHandlerInterface`, which defines methods for `refund()`, `refundStatus()`, and `supports()`, ensuring compatibility and predictable behavior. The core will orchestrate the refund process, validate input, handle errors, and emit events for logging, monitoring, and business logic integration.

This approach ensures consistency across all payment providers, reduces code duplication, and lowers the barrier to entry for new payment extensions. It also enables future enhancements—such as batch refunds, refund auditing, or integration with accounting systems—without requiring changes to individual extensions. The unified refund system will be backward-compatible, allowing legacy extensions to continue functioning while encouraging migration to the standardized interface. By centralizing refund logic in the core, Shopware ensures a reliable, maintainable, and extensible refund experience across all supported payment methods.

## Decision: Use Sphinx with MyST Markdown and autodoc for Documentation Authoring and Hosting

Adopt Sphinx as the primary documentation framework, leveraging MyST Markdown for prose authoring and autodoc for automated reference documentation generation. MyST Markdown provides a modern, markdown-based authoring experience that integrates seamlessly with Sphinx, enabling rich prose documentation with support for reStructuredText features, math, code blocks, and cross-references. This allows technical writers and developers to author content in a familiar, lightweight format while maintaining full compatibility with Sphinx’s powerful build system.

For reference documentation, utilize Sphinx’s autodoc extension to automatically extract API documentation from source code comments (e.g., Google or NumPy-style docstrings). This ensures reference content remains synchronized with the codebase, reducing duplication and the risk of outdated or inaccurate documentation. Combined with the napoleon extension, autodoc supports parsing popular docstring conventions, enabling consistent and readable API reference pages.

Host documentation using Read the Docs, which natively supports Sphinx and MyST Markdown, and provides automated builds, versioning, and search capabilities. Read the Docs integrates with Git repositories (e.g., GitHub, GitLab) to trigger builds on each commit, ensuring documentation is always up to date. The combination of MyST for authoring, autodoc for code-based reference generation, and Read the Docs for hosting provides a scalable, maintainable, and consistent documentation workflow that supports all four documentation forms: explanation (via MyST), tutorial (via structured guides), how-to (via task-oriented sections), and reference (via autodoc). This approach minimizes manual effort, enforces documentation quality, and ensures alignment between code and documentation.

## Decision

The ViewModel will be refactored to accept its dependencies—specifically the UseCase and Rx Schedulers—via constructor injection rather than creating them internally. This enables dependency inversion, allowing unit tests to inject mocked or stubbed implementations of the UseCase and provide test-specific schedulers (e.g., Schedulers.trampoline() for immediate execution). The ViewModel will no longer instantiate the UseCase or rely on hardwired schedulers such as Schedulers.io() or Schedulers.computation(). Instead, it will receive these as parameters in its constructor, making the class more testable, decoupled, and aligned with dependency injection best practices. This change ensures that unit tests can verify the ViewModel’s behavior in isolation by controlling the input data and side effects, without requiring actual network or database operations. Additionally, the use of dependency injection promotes reusability and supports easier integration with frameworks like Dagger or Koin. The testability improvement is critical for maintaining a reliable and maintainable test suite, especially in a reactive architecture where timing and threading are essential to correct behavior. This architectural shift is lightweight and consistent with industry standards for testable Android components.

## Decision

The IITD Architecture team has decided to adopt OpenJDK as the official Java platform for all new and existing IITD applications and infrastructure, effective immediately. This decision is based on a comprehensive evaluation of long-term sustainability, security, compliance, and ecosystem alignment. OpenJDK is selected due to its open-source nature, active community-driven development, full compatibility with Oracle JDK, and the absence of licensing restrictions or commercial fees for production use. The decision supersedes prior reliance on Oracle JDK, which introduces licensing complexity and potential cost implications at scale. By standardizing on OpenJDK, IITD ensures consistent, auditable, and maintainable Java deployments across all systems. All future Java-based projects must use OpenJDK, and existing systems are to be migrated within 12 months. The Infrastructure Team is responsible for providing tooling, build pipelines, and runtime environments that support OpenJDK across all platforms. This decision is final and does not require further approval.

## Decision: Migrate the service from Heroku to GPaaS (Government Platform as a Service) as the long-term hosting environment.

The service has successfully completed its early beta phase on Heroku, enabling rapid delivery and validation of core functionality. With access to GPaaS now confirmed and approved billing in place, the decision is made to migrate the service to GPaaS as its permanent hosting environment. This migration aligns with the long-term strategic goal of operating within a government-approved, secure, and scalable cloud platform that supports compliance with public sector standards, including data sovereignty, security, and resilience requirements.

Heroku served as a valuable short-term solution for rapid iteration and early user feedback, but it is not aligned with the government’s preferred cloud infrastructure for production services. GPaaS offers superior integration with government identity and access management, enhanced monitoring and logging capabilities, and better support for compliance frameworks such as GPGP and ISO 27001. Additionally, GPaaS provides a more sustainable operational model, including predictable cost structures, improved disaster recovery options, and stronger support for ongoing maintenance and upgrades.

The migration will be executed in phases, beginning with a full environment replication, followed by data and configuration transfer, application deployment, and comprehensive validation testing. Post-migration, the service will be monitored closely to ensure performance, reliability, and security meet or exceed current Heroku levels. All future development, deployment, and operational activities will be conducted exclusively within the GPaaS environment, ensuring alignment with government digital standards and long-term maintainability.

## Decision

Implement a globally unique, monotonically increasing sequence number (stream version) for each event within a stream, stored as part of the event metadata. This version number shall be assigned at the time of event creation and must be consistent across all projections and persistence layers. The sequence number must be incremented atomically per stream and must be persisted alongside the event to ensure eventual consistency and deterministic ordering. This version number enables efficient projection replay from a specific point, supports idempotent processing, and allows for synchronization strategies such as waiting for all projections to reach a certain version before acknowledging a write. The sequence number is not derived from timestamps or external sources, but generated via a deterministic, distributed-safe mechanism (e.g., using a centralized sequencer or a conflict-free counter algorithm) to guarantee uniqueness and order. Event stores or databases that support native versioning (e.g., via a `version` field) shall use this field for the stream version. Projections must be designed to consume events based on this version, and any integration events must be tied to the version of the source event. This approach aligns with industry-standard event sourcing patterns and enables advanced use cases such as event sourcing with bounded context, lag monitoring, and safe replay of events. The version field is mandatory and must be validated during event ingestion.

## Decision: Adopt a microservices architecture with containerization using Docker and orchestration via Kubernetes to enable independent deployment, scalability, and resilience of individual application components.

This decision is driven by the need to enhance system agility, improve fault isolation, and support continuous delivery in a complex, evolving application landscape. Monolithic applications have proven increasingly difficult to scale, deploy, and maintain as business requirements grow and teams expand. By decomposing the application into smaller, loosely coupled services, each responsible for a specific business capability, we enable teams to develop, test, and deploy independently without impacting the entire system. Containerization with Docker ensures consistent environments across development, testing, and production, eliminating "it works on my machine" issues. Kubernetes provides the necessary platform for automated deployment, scaling, load balancing, service discovery, and self-healing, allowing the system to dynamically adapt to demand and recover from failures. This architecture also supports polyglot persistence and technology choice per service, enabling optimal use of diverse tools and frameworks. While introducing operational complexity and requiring investment in DevOps practices and observability (logging, monitoring, tracing), the long-term benefits in developer velocity, system reliability, and scalability outweigh the costs. The decision is constrained by the need for strong team coordination, robust CI/CD pipelines, and a mature culture of automation and accountability. This architectural shift is foundational to supporting future growth, enabling rapid innovation, and improving time-to-market for new features.

## Decision

The `core` and `clients` components shall be versioned independently using semantic versioning (SemVer 2.0.0), with the following rules:

1. **Core Versioning**: The `core` library will follow SemVer independently. Breaking changes in the public API of `core` (e.g., removal of functions, changes to interfaces, or modifications to core behavior) will increment the major version. Minor versions will include backward-compatible new features and enhancements. Patch versions will include backward-compatible bug fixes.

2. **Client Versioning**: Each `client` (e.g., OData client, OpenAPI client) will also follow SemVer independently. A client’s version is tied to the specific API it exposes, and its versioning reflects changes in the generated client code, including additions, removals, or modifications to endpoints, data models, or behaviors. Breaking changes in a client (e.g., renaming or removing an endpoint, changing a required parameter) will increment the major version of that client. Minor and patch versions will follow SemVer for backward-compatible additions and fixes.

3. **Dependency Management**: Clients will declare a minimum and maximum version constraint for `core` in their dependencies. The `core` library will not be versioned in lockstep with clients. A client may require `core >= 1.2.0, < 2.0.0` to ensure compatibility with the intended core version.

4. **Version Alignment**: While independent, the `core` and `clients` will be released in coordinated cycles when possible. A new release of `core` will be accompanied by a release of all clients that depend on it, but this is not mandatory. Clients may be updated independently if they only depend on a stable `core` version.

5. **Documentation and Communication**: Version compatibility between `core` and clients will be clearly documented in the release notes and READMEs. A version compatibility matrix will be maintained in the documentation to guide users in selecting compatible versions.

This approach enables independent evolution of `core` and `clients`, supports backward compatibility where possible, and provides clear signals for breaking changes, reducing integration risks.

## Decision: The minimal requirements for an IoT board to support a Home Assistant OS image shall include a 64-bit ARM processor (e.g., Cortex-A53 or higher), at least 512 MB of RAM, 4 GB of onboard storage (e.g., eMMC or SPI-NAND), and support for secure boot with a hardware-backed Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The board must also provide a reliable, low-power Ethernet interface or Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) with support for WPA3, and a standardized, accessible GPIO interface for peripheral integration. The firmware must be deliverable via a secure, signed OTA update mechanism using a dual-partition scheme to ensure rollback capability. All boards must be provisioned with a unique, hardware-derived identity (e.g., via a secure element or embedded key) to enable secure device registration and long-term integrity verification.

For legacy or replaced board generations, a backward compatibility policy shall be enforced: Home Assistant OS will support the latest two generations of hardware, with each generation receiving security updates and critical bug fixes for a minimum of three years from its initial release. Boards older than the two most recent generations will be marked as unsupported and will no longer receive updates, but the OS image will continue to boot with a clear warning message indicating end-of-life status. A migration path must be provided via a dedicated, documented upgrade guide and a user-friendly tool to transfer configuration and integrations to a supported board. The Home Assistant OS image will include a hardware compatibility layer that checks for supported boards at boot time and refuses to run on unsupported hardware unless explicitly overridden in developer mode. This ensures a balance between security, long-term maintainability, and user flexibility.

## Decision: Adopt a stateless architecture for Identity, Metadata, and Storage services with distributed, persistent backing stores, enabling horizontal scalability and cloud-agnostic deployment.

To achieve cloud-agnostic scalability, the Identity, Metadata, and Storage components will be redesigned to be stateless, with all persistent data stored in external, distributed systems. Identity and metadata will be managed through a scalable, replicated database (e.g., PostgreSQL with streaming replication or a cloud-agnostic managed database like CockroachDB) accessible via standard protocols. Storage will be abstracted using a distributed object store (e.g., S3-compatible storage) with consistent hashing and eventual consistency, allowing any instance to access data regardless of location. All service instances will be identical and bootable from a minimal image, with no local state or file system dependencies. Configuration and runtime state will be managed externally via a dedicated configuration service or etcd-style key-value store. This decoupling enables the system to be deployed across any cloud provider or on-premises environment using container orchestration (e.g., Kubernetes), with auto-scaling and load balancing handled at the infrastructure layer. The architecture will support multi-region deployments with data replication and failover, ensuring high availability and resilience. This design eliminates vendor lock-in, supports dynamic scaling, and aligns with modern cloud-native patterns, fulfilling the engineering goal of cloud agnosticism while enabling robust, scalable operation.

## Decision: Adopt a standardized code formatting and style enforcement tool across the entire codebase, using Prettier for JavaScript/TypeScript and ESLint with a shared configuration for linting rules. All developers must integrate these tools into their development environment via pre-commit hooks (using Husky) to automatically format code and enforce style checks before every commit. The configuration will be stored in the repository root and version-controlled, ensuring consistency across all environments. Additionally, a CI/CD pipeline step will be added to reject pull requests that fail the formatting or linting checks, guaranteeing that only code meeting the defined standards is merged. This approach eliminates subjective style debates, reduces merge conflicts related to formatting, and ensures a uniform codebase appearance, significantly improving readability and maintainability for all contributors.

## Decision

The low-level functions of the DiamondSquare module (e.g., `step`, `diamond`, `square`, `interpolate`) shall be made private and hidden from the public API. Only the high-level, user-facing functions `new/1`, `step_to_end/1`, and `grid/1` shall be exported. This ensures a clean, safe, and intentional interface that prevents users from directly manipulating internal state or invoking intermediate steps that could lead to inconsistent or incorrect terrain generation. The internal state of the DiamondSquare struct is encapsulated, and all mutations are performed through the well-defined `step_to_end/1` function, which guarantees a complete and correct execution path. This decision reduces cognitive load on users, eliminates the risk of misuse, and simplifies both documentation and testing. The implementation details, including the iterative refinement process and coordinate management, are fully internal and subject to change without breaking the public contract. Tests will focus exclusively on the public interface, ensuring correctness through observable behavior rather than internal implementation. This approach aligns with the principle of information hiding and supports long-term maintainability and evolution of the module.

## Decision: Adopt a State Machine Pattern with Lifecycle Definitions as First-Class Concepts

To abstractly model the semantically meaningful lifetime and state transitions of resources, the platform shall implement a State Machine pattern where lifecycle definitions are first-class, configurable entities. Each resource type will be associated with a lifecycle definition that explicitly defines its valid states, permissible transitions between states, and the conditions or triggers (e.g., time-based, user action, system event) that cause transitions. These lifecycle definitions will be modeled as declarative configuration (e.g., JSON or YAML) or domain-specific language (DSL) artifacts, decoupling the business logic of state management from the core resource implementation. The state machine will enforce transitions through a centralized transition engine that validates actions against the current state and defined rules before allowing state changes. This approach enables the platform to support diverse use-cases—such as data retention, archival, deletion, or compliance workflows—by simply registering different lifecycle definitions per resource type or tenant, without modifying core logic. Furthermore, the state machine will be extensible with hooks for side effects (e.g., notifications, audit logging, data migration) at state boundaries, ensuring observability and consistency. By treating lifecycles as configuration rather than code, the platform achieves flexibility, maintainability, and reusability across domains, while ensuring semantic correctness and auditability of resource lifetimes.

## Decision: Adopt a Vertical Micro-Frontends Architecture for Hackney’s Single-View Application

We will adopt a vertical micro-frontend architecture, where each business domain (e.g., Housing, Benefits, Council Tax) is owned by a dedicated team and corresponds to a single micro-frontend per page. This approach aligns with business ownership, enables autonomous development and deployment, and reduces cognitive load by maintaining clear boundaries between domains.

The container application will be responsible for rendering shared UI elements (header, footer, navigation), managing global state (authentication, user session), and orchestrating the loading and mounting of the appropriate micro-frontend based on the route. Each micro-frontend will be developed, tested, and deployed independently, using its own build pipeline and versioning, while adhering to shared contracts for integration (e.g., agreed-upon API for data and events).

We reject the horizontal approach due to the increased complexity in ensuring visual consistency, coordination between teams, and potential for inconsistent UX when multiple micro-frontends render side-by-side. The vertical model provides a simpler, more maintainable path to scalable frontend architecture, with clear ownership, reduced code duplication, and improved performance through on-demand loading.

To enable this, we will implement a modular container using a framework-agnostic approach (e.g., via Web Components or a lightweight runtime like Module Federation), ensuring compatibility with existing tech stacks (React, Redux) while allowing future flexibility. Shared libraries will be managed via a centralized monorepo or package registry, with versioning and backward compatibility enforced.

This decision enables faster development cycles, reduces technical debt, and improves the end-user experience by eliminating full page reloads while maintaining a cohesive, performant application.

## Decision: Use a modular, format-agnostic output engine with a pluggable backend architecture for rendering ADRs.

To maximize usability of adr-viewer while preserving flexibility for future output formats—including live web servers—adopt a modular architecture where the core ADR processor is decoupled from the output rendering layer. The system will treat rendering as a pluggable component, with a clear interface defining how ADRs are transformed into a final format (e.g., HTML, Markdown, JSON, or live HTML with server-side rendering). This allows the core logic to remain focused on parsing, validating, and organizing ADRs, while output-specific behavior is encapsulated in separate, interchangeable backends.

The default output format will be static HTML, ensuring immediate usability across platforms without dependencies. However, additional backends—such as a live web server with dynamic rendering, a CLI output format, or a JSON schema for programmatic access—can be developed as optional plugins. This approach enables future extensibility without compromising the stability or simplicity of the primary use case.

All output backends will implement a shared interface (e.g., `render(adr: ADR, context: RenderContext)`), ensuring consistent behavior and easing maintenance. Configuration will determine which backend is used at runtime, allowing users to switch formats via a simple flag or configuration file. The system will support both file-based rendering and streaming output, enabling use in CI/CD pipelines, local development, and production web environments.

This design ensures that adr-viewer remains lightweight, user-friendly, and future-proof, while allowing the team to incrementally introduce new output formats without refactoring the core logic. It also promotes reusability: the same ADR data model can be rendered in multiple ways, supporting diverse user needs—from documentation generation to interactive web-based ADR exploration.

## Decision: Adopt a consistent, nouns-based resource naming convention and strictly adhere to REST semantics for HTTP methods.

Resource names in the API shall be plural, lowercase, and use clear, unambiguous nouns that represent collections of entities (e.g., `/users`, `/orders`, `/products`). Singular resource names are prohibited to maintain consistency and align with REST best practices. Hierarchical relationships between resources shall be represented through path composition (e.g., `/users/{userId}/orders`) only when logically appropriate and semantically correct.

HTTP methods shall be used strictly according to their intended semantics:
- `GET` for retrieving representations of resources or collections.
- `POST` for creating new resources within a collection.
- `PUT` for replacing an entire resource at a specific identifier.
- `PATCH` for applying partial updates to a resource.
- `DELETE` for removing a resource.

Actions that do not represent resource state changes or are not idempotent (e.g., "activate", "refund", "sendEmail") shall not be exposed as top-level endpoints. Instead, such operations shall be modeled as sub-resources or embedded in the request body via `POST` or `PATCH`, or implemented as separate, well-documented operations with appropriate verbs, provided they are state-changing and idempotent where applicable.

All endpoints shall be versioned via a URL path prefix (e.g., `/v1/users`) to support backward compatibility and future evolution. The API shall not use query parameters to represent resource identifiers or to trigger actions that are not idempotent or read-only.

This decision ensures clarity, predictability, and interoperability with standard tools and clients, while enabling maintainable and scalable API evolution.

## Decision

To ensure PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) support across cloud providers lacking native storage integration, Compliant Kubernetes will adopt a standardized, cloud-agnostic storage solution based on Longhorn. Longhorn is selected as the default persistent storage provider due to its lightweight architecture, native Kubernetes integration, resilience, and compliance-ready features such as data encryption, audit logging, and backup/restore capabilities. Longhorn will be deployed as a cluster-level operator within the Compliant Kubernetes control plane, enabling automatic provisioning and management of PersistentVolumes (PVs) without requiring cloud-specific storage drivers. This approach ensures consistent storage behavior across all target clouds, including those with no native storage support. To maintain compliance, Longhorn will be configured with default security settings (e.g., encrypted volumes, role-based access control, and secure volume snapshots), and its operations will be auditable via Kubernetes event logs and external compliance tools. Additionally, the Compliant Kubernetes operator will enforce policy-driven storage classes that align with regulatory requirements, allowing administrators to define storage profiles (e.g., "high-availability", "encrypted-only") that are enforced at the PVC creation level. For environments where Longhorn is unsuitable, a fallback mechanism will allow the use of in-tree storage providers (e.g., hostPath, emptyDir) only when explicitly permitted by compliance policy, with strict runtime monitoring to prevent unauthorized usage. This strategy enables reliable, secure, and compliant PVC support across all target clouds, fulfilling the vision of multi-cloud, open-source, and compliant Kubernetes.

## Decision: Use JavaScript as the primary client-side programming language for Libero Reviewer

We have decided to use JavaScript as the primary client-side programming language for Libero Reviewer. This decision is based on several key factors. First, JavaScript is the only language natively supported by all modern web browsers, ensuring broad compatibility and consistent behavior across platforms and devices. This is critical for Libero Reviewer, which must function reliably in diverse user environments, including desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

Second, JavaScript enables rich, interactive user experiences through dynamic DOM manipulation, event handling, and real-time updates—essential for a review system that requires responsive feedback, live collaboration, and seamless form interactions. The availability of mature, well-supported frameworks and libraries (such as React, Vue, or Angular) allows us to build scalable, maintainable, and performant user interfaces while leveraging community-driven tooling, best practices, and extensive documentation.

Third, the ecosystem surrounding JavaScript—including package managers (npm/yarn), build tools (Webpack, Vite), testing frameworks (Jest, Cypress), and static analysis tools (ESLint)—provides a robust foundation for modern development workflows. This ecosystem supports rapid iteration, code quality assurance, and efficient deployment, which aligns with our goals for agility and maintainability.

Finally, the widespread expertise in JavaScript among developers ensures a larger talent pool, faster onboarding, and easier long-term maintenance. Given these advantages in compatibility, performance, ecosystem maturity, and developer accessibility, JavaScript is the optimal choice for implementing the client-side logic of Libero Reviewer.

## Decision: Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk for application deployment

We will use AWS Elastic Beanstalk as the primary deployment mechanism for our application. Elastic Beanstalk provides a fully managed platform that abstracts away the underlying infrastructure, allowing us to focus on application code rather than server configuration, scaling, or load balancing. It supports multiple programming languages (including Java, Python, Node.js, Ruby, Go, and PHP), enabling flexibility in our technology stack while maintaining consistent deployment behavior across environments.

Elastic Beanstalk automatically handles provisioning, load balancing, auto-scaling, and monitoring, reducing operational overhead and minimizing the risk of misconfiguration. It integrates seamlessly with AWS services such as RDS for databases, S3 for storage, and CloudWatch for logging and metrics. The deployment process is streamlined via versioned application packages (ZIP or WAR files) or direct Git integration, enabling CI/CD workflows using tools like AWS CodePipeline or GitHub Actions.

We will maintain separate environments (e.g., development, staging, production) using Elastic Beanstalk environments, each with its own configuration, environment variables, and resource isolation. This ensures safe testing and gradual rollout of changes. Environment-specific settings will be managed through configuration files (e.g., `.ebextensions`) and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for sensitive data.

By choosing Elastic Beanstalk, we achieve rapid deployment, consistent environment behavior, built-in scalability, and reduced operational burden—enabling our team to deliver features faster with higher reliability and lower risk of deployment failures.

## Decision

Disable S3 versioning on the Fedora-backed S3 bucket and instead implement cross-region replication (CRR) using S3's built-in CRR feature without versioning enabled. This decision resolves the 403 permission errors encountered during file uploads, reads, and access via Cantaloupe by eliminating the complexities introduced by versioned object handling in Fedora and Cantaloupe, which are not designed to manage multiple object versions seamlessly. While versioning is required for CRR in some configurations, S3 CRR can operate effectively with versioning disabled if the replication is configured at the bucket level with a replication role that grants sufficient permissions to the source and destination buckets. By disabling versioning and relying on CRR with a replication policy, we maintain data durability and geographic redundancy without introducing the permission and metadata inconsistencies that arise from versioned object access. This approach simplifies the interaction between Fedora, Cantaloupe, and S3, ensuring consistent object access semantics and eliminating the need for version-aware handling in downstream systems. The trade-off is that versioned object recovery (e.g., restoring a previous version) is no longer available, but this is acceptable given that Fedora manages its own versioning through its internal object model, and the primary goal—geographic redundancy—is still met via CRR. This change will be accompanied by a thorough review of the replication policy, access control (IAM and bucket policies), and validation of file access workflows in both primary and replicated regions.

## Decision

Arachne shall adopt a dependency-aware, lifecycle-managed bootstrapping system based on a declarative service graph, where all application and module-defined components (services, configurations, etc.) are registered as named, dependency-injected lifecycle entities. The bootstrapping process is structured into three phases: (1) configuration resolution and dependency graph construction, (2) service startup in topological order (depth-first, respecting dependencies), and (3) service shutdown in reverse topological order. Each service declares its dependencies via a static, compile-time contract (e.g., `:depends-on [other-service]` in configuration or via metadata), and the framework resolves these into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) at startup. Services are instantiated via a dependency-injection container (e.g., using `clojure.spec` or `integrant`-style configuration), with initialization and shutdown functions (e.g., `start!`, `stop!`) invoked automatically in the correct order. The framework ensures that no service is started before its dependencies are ready, and no service is stopped before it is safely shut down. This model is exposed via a minimal, idiomatic API for module and application authors to define and register services, with hooks for pre- and post-initialization logic. Shutdown is guaranteed to be graceful and deterministic, even in the face of failures, by using a try-catch-and-stop-all mechanism that ensures all running services are stopped in reverse dependency order. This approach provides predictable, composable, and safe initialization and termination of all system components, enabling modular, extensible, and maintainable application bootstrapping.

## Decision

We will use a declarative dependency specification format (e.g., `package.json` for JavaScript, `requirements.txt` for Python, or `Cargo.toml` for Rust) to represent package dependencies. This approach is preferred over an imperative or procedural method because it clearly defines the required packages and their versions in a human-readable, version-controlled format. This enables consistent and reproducible builds across environments, supports automated dependency resolution and verification, and integrates seamlessly with package managers and CI/CD pipelines. It also simplifies auditing, dependency tracking, and security scanning by providing a single source of truth for all required packages. Using a declarative format ensures that dependency installation is idempotent, deterministic, and aligned with industry best practices, reducing the risk of environment drift and configuration errors.

## Decision: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller as the primary ingress and load balancing solution for the EKS cluster, managing both ALBs for Ingress resources and NLBs for Service resources, while maintaining support for both Ingress and Service Kubernetes resources to ensure flexibility in handling L4 and L7 traffic, TLS termination, and integration with AWS Route 53. The controller will be deployed via the official Helm chart with appropriate IAM roles and permissions, enabling automated provisioning and management of AWS load balancers. This approach aligns with Kubernetes’ deprecation of in-tree cloud providers and leverages the AWS Load Balancer Controller’s native support for ALB and NLB provisioning, including advanced features such as TLS termination, path-based routing, and integration with Route 53 via DNS names. To ensure compatibility with the existing GOV.UK Router service, the cluster will initially be configured to operate in a hybrid mode where Ingress and Service resources are used selectively based on routing requirements, with clear documentation and operational boundaries established between the router and the AWS Load Balancer Controller. This enables a phased evaluation of overlap and eventual decoupling or integration as needed. The use of Ingress resources for L7 traffic and Service resources of type LoadBalancer for L4 traffic ensures full support for use cases including name-based virtual hosting, HTTP to HTTPS redirection, and direct access to backend services, while maintaining a secure, managed, and scalable architecture.

## Decision

We will adopt Option 2: a dedicated Search Bounded Context exposing a unified search endpoint with a centralized AWS ElasticSearch instance, maintaining one index per domain requiring search functionality. This decision is based on the need for cross-domain search capabilities, such as querying people, assets, and tenures in combination, which requires aggregating data across bounded contexts. A centralized search index enables consistent, performant, and scalable advanced search (including free text, partial matching, wildcards, and filters) across multiple domains, while avoiding data duplication and inconsistency risks present in decentralized indexes. It also simplifies maintenance, monitoring, and security management of the search infrastructure under a single AWS ElasticSearch domain. While Option 1 may be suitable for isolated domain-level searches, the architectural requirement for inter-domain search, combined with the need for a unified and future-proof search layer, makes a centralized approach more aligned with Hackney’s long-term goals. The London Region availability of AWS ElasticSearch further validates this choice. The Search Bounded Context will be responsible for synchronizing domain data (via event-driven updates or batch processes) into its respective indexes, ensuring search results remain consistent with the source data. This design supports eventual consistency, scalability, and extensibility as new domains are added to the search surface.

## Decision: Implement a flux redundancy and observability analysis to guide measurement selection and ensure a well-constrained system.

To address the ambiguity in defining independent fluxes and the risk of over- or under-constrained systems, Maud shall incorporate a pre-processing flux analysis module that evaluates the structural observability and redundancy of measured fluxes within a metabolic network. This module will compute the rank of the stoichiometric matrix restricted to measured reactions, identifying linear dependencies among fluxes and flagging redundant measurements. It will also detect underdetermined configurations by assessing the number of independent flux measurements relative to the degrees of freedom in the network. Based on this analysis, Maud will provide actionable recommendations: either suggest a minimal set of independent flux measurements to ensure a well-constrained system, or highlight missing fluxes that would improve identifiability. This analysis will be integrated into the Bayesian inference pipeline, ensuring that prior information and likelihoods are informed by a principled assessment of data quality and structural information content. The decision to measure a flux will thus be guided by its contribution to system observability, not merely its biological relevance, thereby preventing over-parameterization and improving posterior inference reliability.

## Decision

Adopt a modern, containerized full-stack architecture using Node.js with Express for the backend, React for the frontend, and WebSocket via Socket.IO, hosted on Heroku. This approach replaces the legacy Python/Flask implementation to address reliability issues with socket connections, improve maintainability, and enable easier deployment and future extensibility. Node.js provides superior performance for real-time communication, which is critical for DECODE’s interactive components, while its rich ecosystem of tools and libraries simplifies development and debugging. Express offers a lightweight, flexible foundation for building scalable APIs, and the use of Socket.IO ensures robust, cross-platform WebSocket support with automatic fallbacks, reducing the risk of the intermittent socket failures experienced in the Python version. The frontend will be built with React, enabling a responsive, component-based UI that can be easily extended with features like user authentication, logging, and dashboard enhancements. All services will be containerized using Docker, with a well-defined `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` for consistent local and production environments. Deployment will leverage Heroku’s Git-based workflow, which supports automatic builds, environment variable management, and seamless scaling. This stack ensures the demo app is easy to deploy publicly, maintainable through modular code organization and clear separation of concerns, and highly extensible—adding new features such as user login or logging will be straightforward using established patterns (e.g., JWT authentication, logging middleware, and React context for state management). This decision balances performance, reliability, developer experience, and long-term maintainability, fulfilling all requirements for a production-ready, demonstrable DECODE system.

## Decision

We have selected the **Excelize** package over XLSX for parsing XLSX files in the Rate Engine. Excelize offers superior performance, comprehensive support for modern XLSX features (including cell formatting, formulas, and conditional formatting), and better stability when handling large or complex Excel files. It also provides a more intuitive and consistent API for reading and writing Excel files, reducing the likelihood of parsing errors. Additionally, Excelize is actively maintained with regular updates and a strong community, ensuring long-term reliability and security. The package supports both reading and writing, which future-proofs the solution for potential export or transformation needs. While XLSX is simpler and lightweight, it lacks the robustness and feature set required for accurate and reliable parsing of the 400NG Tariff baseline rates document, which includes structured data, multiple sheets, and formatting critical for validation. Therefore, Excelize is the optimal choice for ensuring data integrity, maintainability, and scalability in the rate import pipeline.

## Decision: Adopt a modern, component-based full-stack JavaScript framework (React.js for the frontend, Node.js with Express for the backend) paired with a relational database (PostgreSQL) and a GraphQL API layer, enabling flexible data modeling, user-based contributions, complex search capabilities, and long-term maintainability.

The decision to use React.js, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, and GraphQL was driven by the need for a scalable, maintainable, and extensible architecture that supports the Institute’s long-term vision for the Schoenberg Database of Manuscripts. React.js provides a component-driven UI framework that allows for reusable, testable, and modular frontend development, essential for building a rich, interactive user experience with dynamic search and editing interfaces. Node.js and Express offer a performant, event-driven runtime with strong ecosystem support for building scalable APIs, while also enabling seamless integration with modern frontend tooling and DevOps practices.

PostgreSQL was selected as the primary database due to its robust support for complex data types, JSONB fields, full-text search, and extensible schema design—critical for modeling diverse manuscript metadata, relationships, and hierarchical structures. Its strong ACID compliance and support for user roles and permissions align with the requirement for secure, user-based editing and contribution workflows.

GraphQL was adopted as the API layer to provide flexible, efficient data querying and mutation capabilities. It enables clients to request only the data they need, reducing payload size and improving performance, especially under complex search and filtering scenarios. It also supports real-time updates via subscriptions and facilitates versioning and evolution of the data model without breaking existing integrations.

Together, this stack ensures the new SDBM is future-proof, supports incremental feature development, and aligns with modern software engineering practices—enabling the Institute to manage complex manuscript data, support user contributions securely, deliver advanced search functionality, and maintain the system efficiently over the three-year grant period and beyond.

## Decision: Decompose the monolithic Hamlet engine Docker image into a set of lightweight, purpose-specific Docker images, each responsible for a single component or function (e.g., Bash scripting, Freemarker templating, Java runtime), and manage their orchestration via a declarative composition tool such as Docker Compose or Kubernetes. Use versioned image tags and immutable image builds to enable safe, repeatable deployment of different Hamlet versions. Replace the current git-based code collection process with a dependency management approach using artifact repositories (e.g., Docker Hub, Nexus, or JFrog) to fetch pre-built, tested, and validated component images. This decoupling allows independent versioning, scaling, and reuse of components, reduces image size, improves security posture through smaller attack surface, and enables parallel development and deployment workflows. The build and deploy pipeline will be restructured to compose the required components at runtime based on configuration, eliminating the need to rebuild and redeploy the entire image for version changes.

## Decision: Implement a standardized, server-to-server subscription status verification mechanism using signed JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) issued by the Subscription Provider, with the Relying Party validating the JWT's signature and claims to determine user entitlements.

The Relying Party will receive a signed JWT from the Subscription Provider at regular intervals (e.g., upon user login or at scheduled refresh intervals) or on-demand when user status changes. The JWT will contain essential claims such as `sub` (user identifier), `subscription_status` (e.g., active, expired, trial), `plan_id`, `start_date`, `end_date`, and `iat` (issued at). The JWT will be signed using a cryptographic key pair (e.g., RS256) managed by the Subscription Provider, with the public key made available to the Relying Party via a well-known endpoint (e.g., `/well-known/jwks.json`).

The Relying Party will validate the JWT’s signature using the provider’s public key, verify the issuer (`iss` claim), ensure the token is not expired (`exp` claim), and check the `subscription_status` claim to determine feature access. This approach ensures secure, tamper-proof, and verifiable status updates without requiring the Relying Party to maintain or trust a local state of subscription data. It supports scalability, reduces latency by eliminating the need for real-time polling, and enables seamless integration with existing authentication and authorization infrastructure. The use of standardized JWTs ensures interoperability across systems and simplifies implementation across multiple Relying Parties.

## Decision: Implement a dynamic route discovery mechanism using a combination of network topology polling and event-driven updates via BGP or OSPF protocol integration, alongside a centralized route synchronization service. The system will periodically scan the network for newly advertised routes and immediately process route updates received through standardized routing protocols. Discovered routes will be automatically validated against predefined policy rules (e.g., prefix length, AS path, origin) before being added to the routing table. A summary route generation service will be enabled by default, aggregating eligible individual routes into supernet entries based on administrative and performance criteria. All route changes—both discovered and summarized—will be synchronized across all relevant nodes through a distributed state management system using consensus-based replication (e.g., Raft or Paxos) to ensure consistency and fault tolerance. This approach eliminates manual configuration, reduces the risk of missed routes, and maintains routing integrity while supporting scalability and operational resilience. The solution prioritizes reliability by ensuring that dynamic route discovery does not override static or explicitly configured routes unless explicitly permitted by policy, and provides audit logging and real-time monitoring for traceability and compliance.

## Decision: Implement automated test execution as part of the CI/CD pipeline with mandatory test coverage thresholds.

To maintain high test coverage without relying on manual checks, we will integrate automated test execution into the CI/CD pipeline. Every code change submitted via pull request will trigger a build that includes running all unit, integration, and end-to-end tests. Test coverage will be measured using a code coverage tool (e.g., Istanbul, JaCoCo, or similar) and reported as part of the build process. A minimum coverage threshold (e.g., 80% for unit tests, 70% for integration tests) will be enforced; builds will fail if coverage drops below this threshold. Coverage reports will be generated and made accessible to the team, with detailed breakdowns by file and test type. This ensures that coverage is consistently monitored and enforced at every stage of development, eliminating the risk of human oversight. Additionally, coverage trends will be tracked over time using a dedicated dashboard to identify regressions and guide improvement efforts. By automating coverage enforcement and reporting, we eliminate manual checks, reduce human error, and maintain a reliable, high-quality codebase.

## Decision: Use hpack to generate Cabal files instead of writing them manually

Adopt hpack as the standard tool for generating Cabal files in all new and existing Haskell projects. hpack eliminates redundancy by allowing declarative, YAML-based configuration that automatically infers common build settings, such as exposed modules, dependencies, and GHC options. This removes the need to manually specify `ghc-options` for each target, duplicate common dependencies across multiple targets, or enumerate every exposed module explicitly. hpack’s convention-over-configuration approach reduces boilerplate, minimizes errors from manual repetition, and improves maintainability. The configuration is more concise, readable, and easier to version-control. Projects using hpack benefit from consistent build setup across targets and seamless integration with modern Haskell tooling like `cabal new-build`, `cabal v2-build`, and `stack`. The decision to use hpack is fully aligned with current best practices in the Haskell ecosystem and significantly improves developer experience by reducing friction in dependency management, module exposure, and build configuration.

## Decision: Migrate download functionality to use the Android MediaStore API and adopt scoped storage best practices for Android SDK 30 and above.

To ensure compatibility with Android SDK 30 and above, the download feature must be refactored to operate within the constraints of scoped storage. Direct access to external storage via `Environment.getExternalStorageDirectory()` and related paths is deprecated and restricted. Instead, downloads will be managed through the MediaStore API, which provides a consistent and secure way to insert media files (e.g., images, videos, audio) into the device’s shared storage while respecting the scoped storage model.

All file downloads will be performed using `ContentResolver.insert()` with the appropriate MediaStore URI (e.g., `MediaStore.Downloads.EXTERNAL_CONTENT_URI`), and the resulting `ContentValues` will include metadata such as display name, MIME type, and relative path. The download process will be initiated via `ContentResolver.openOutputStream()` to write the file data securely.

For applications requiring user-level control over file selection (e.g., saving to specific directories), the `Storage Access Framework (SAF)` will be integrated using `Intent.ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE` to allow users to grant explicit access to a directory. This ensures compliance with scoped storage while preserving user intent and flexibility.

Additionally, the app’s `AndroidManifest.xml` will be updated to include the `android:requestLegacyExternalStorage="false"` attribute (default behavior for SDK 30+), and all file operations will be audited to ensure they do not rely on legacy external storage access. Permissions such as `READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` and `WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE` will be removed from the manifest unless required for non-scoped use cases (e.g., accessing app-specific files), and runtime permission checks will be replaced with appropriate `ContentResolver` operations.

This approach ensures full compliance with Android 11+ storage policies, enables future app updates beyond November 2021, and maintains user data privacy and security.

## Decision: The proxy node will be deployed on the GDS Supported Platform (GSP), leveraging Kubernetes running on AWS instances with Docker containerisation. All proxy node instances must be provisioned exclusively via the GSP’s CI/CD pipeline, ensuring consistent configuration, security hardening, and auditability. Only Docker images signed with a GDS-approved cryptographic key are permitted for deployment, enforced through image signing validation at the Kubernetes admission control layer (e.g., using cosign and image policy webhooks). Co-location of proxy node containers with other applications is prohibited; each proxy node deployment must run in a dedicated Kubernetes namespace with strict network policies and pod security standards (e.g., using Pod Security Admission and NetworkPolicy). The GSP’s built-in monitoring, logging, and logging aggregation (e.g., via Fluentd and Prometheus) will be utilised to meet operational and compliance requirements. All configuration, secrets, and infrastructure-as-code are managed through the GSP’s approved tooling (e.g., GitOps with ArgoCD), ensuring traceability and consistency across environments. This approach ensures the proxy node adheres to GDS internal hosting requirements, maintains isolation, enforces secure image deployment, and aligns with the GSP’s operational and security standards.

## Decision

Store pixel data in single precision (float32) on disk and extend to double precision (float64) only during arithmetic operations within algorithmic chains that involve long sequences of function calls, such as those in TobyFit. This approach minimizes the accumulation of rounding errors by ensuring that intermediate computations are performed with higher precision, preserving the qualitative fidelity of results. Data will be converted to double precision immediately before entering such computational chains and reverted to single precision after completion, minimizing memory overhead and maintaining performance benefits for subsequent operations. Performance-critical operations will be executed on single-precision data when possible, leveraging the speed advantages of float32 arithmetic. To ensure consistency between MATLAB and C++ implementations of pixel binning, both will be required to use the same precision-aware binning logic: perform binning in double precision during computation and only cast to single precision upon final output. This guarantees identical results across platforms and prevents divergence due to rounding differences. The use of single precision for storage balances memory efficiency and performance while preserving numerical accuracy through controlled precision extension during critical computation phases.

## Decision

Adopt a containerized, isolated test execution environment using Docker-in-Docker (DinD) with ephemeral test databases and mocked external services, replacing the current shared, stateful test infrastructure. This approach will eliminate environmental inconsistencies, reduce flakiness caused by test interference, and improve test reliability. We will implement test-specific, disposable database instances (e.g., PostgreSQL via Docker) and use service virtualization tools like WireMock or Mountebank for external dependencies. All test runs will be executed in a clean, reproducible container environment with no shared state between runs. We will also introduce deterministic test execution by enforcing strict ordering of test setup, using unique test data per run, and applying idempotent test cleanup. To address CI credit usage, we will integrate test flakiness detection via test metadata and retry logic with exponential backoff for failed tests, reducing redundant runs. This stack will be instrumented with real-time test reliability metrics and integrated into our CI pipeline to flag unstable tests and prevent merge until reliability thresholds are met. The new stack will be rolled out incrementally across services, with a 90-day performance review to validate improvements in success rate, credit usage, and developer velocity. This decision balances immediate reliability gains with long-term maintainability, enabling a sustainable path toward continuous delivery.

## Decision

Do not call `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()` in catch blocks for `InterruptedException` when using JUnit, even if it suppresses SonarQube warnings. Instead, rethrow the `InterruptedException` or wrap it in a `RuntimeException` with a descriptive message, preserving the original interrupt status. This approach maintains thread interruption semantics correctly while avoiding the side effects caused by JUnit's thread reuse. By rethrowing the exception, the interruption is propagated up the call stack where it can be handled appropriately by higher-level logic, such as test framework cleanup or asynchronous task cancellation. This pattern ensures that the interrupt status is not lost and avoids the unpredictable test failures that occur when `Thread.interrupt()` is called directly in a test context. SonarQube can be configured to ignore RSPEC-2142 in test classes or specific methods where interruption handling is managed safely through rethrowing, using a `@SuppressWarnings("squid:S2142")` annotation with a clear justification. This balances static analysis requirements with runtime correctness and test stability.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, automated code style and quality enforcement pipeline using industry-leading tools: **ESLint** for JavaScript/TypeScript linting with a well-maintained, opinionated preset (e.g., `eslint:recommended` + `eslint-plugin-prettier`), **Prettier** for consistent code formatting, and **EditorConfig** for editor-level consistency across team members. Integrate these tools into the development workflow via pre-commit hooks using **Husky** and **lint-staged**, ensuring that code is automatically formatted and linted before every commit. Additionally, enforce code quality in CI/CD pipelines using **GitHub Actions** or equivalent, blocking merges if linting or formatting rules are violated. This approach eliminates subjective style debates, ensures consistency across all contributors and repositories, and embeds best practices directly into the development process—making adherence effortless and automatic. All configuration will be version-controlled, shared, and maintained in a central `eslint.config.js`, `.prettierrc`, and `.editorconfig` file, with clear documentation in the project’s README. This stack is proven at scale across major open-source and enterprise projects, offers excellent IDE integration, and reduces cognitive load by removing manual style decisions.

## Decision: Adoption of Kubernetes as the Container Orchestration Platform

To achieve scalability, full automation, resilience, and fault tolerance in the microservices architecture, Kubernetes was selected as the primary container orchestration platform. Kubernetes provides declarative configuration, automated deployment, scaling, and self-healing capabilities, directly addressing the core requirements. Its built-in load balancing, service discovery, and rolling updates enable seamless handling of variable workloads while minimizing downtime. The platform’s native support for health checks, automatic restarts of failed containers, and pod replication ensures fault tolerance and eliminates single points of failure when properly configured. Furthermore, Kubernetes integrates with automated CI/CD pipelines, enabling fully automated deployment and lifecycle management. Its rich ecosystem of operators, custom resources, and monitoring tools (e.g., Prometheus, Grafana) supports operational visibility and proactive failure detection. By leveraging Kubernetes, the system can scale horizontally based on metrics, recover from node or pod failures automatically, and maintain high availability across distributed environments. This decision establishes a consistent, repeatable, and production-grade foundation for all microservices, ensuring long-term maintainability and resilience.

## Decision

To resolve the inability to amend configuration via the UI during reconnection attempts, we will implement a non-blocking, asynchronous configuration update mechanism that decouples the UI configuration apply operation from the synchronized lifecycle state transitions of individual connections. Specifically, we will introduce a dedicated configuration management layer that operates independently of the core component lifecycle, allowing configuration changes to be queued and processed in a background thread without blocking the initialization or reconnection phases of any connection.

This layer will validate and serialize configuration updates, apply them to the runtime state of components without requiring a full restart, and provide immediate feedback to the UI. For components that require a restart (e.g., connections), the system will defer the restart until the connection is no longer in a blocked initialization state, or until a configurable timeout is reached, at which point a best-effort restart will be attempted.

Additionally, we will modify the UI to detect when a reconnection loop is active and present a warning state, indicating that configuration changes may be delayed, while still allowing the user to submit updates. The UI will not wait for full system startup or completion of reconnection attempts, but instead report the status of configuration application asynchronously.

This approach ensures that the UI remains responsive, configuration can be applied even during reconnection loops, and the core reconnection logic is not disrupted by external state changes. The change is backward compatible and introduces minimal performance overhead, while solving the root cause: synchronization blocking due to lifecycle phase dependencies.

## Decision: Use an external Lucene-based fulltext indexing service, integrated as a non-blocking, optional component with fallback behavior.

Implement fulltext search using a dedicated Lucene-backed indexing service, hosted as a separate, optional component that runs alongside docspell. This service will be responsible for indexing document contents asynchronously after document ingestion, ensuring that the core document management functionality remains unaffected by indexing performance or failures. The integration will be designed to be non-blocking: document operations (upload, retrieval, metadata updates) will proceed normally even if the index is unavailable or temporarily failing. The system will log indexing errors but not propagate them as failures to the main application flow.

The Lucene-based index will be managed via a lightweight, embedded service (e.g., using Apache Lucene directly or a minimal wrapper such as `lucene-indexer`), avoiding reliance on a full external search engine like Elasticsearch unless scalability demands arise. This ensures minimal resource overhead and avoids introducing complex distributed systems for a feature that is not central to the application's core function.

To maintain system resilience, the application will detect the absence or failure of the indexing service and gracefully degrade, disabling fulltext search queries while continuing to serve documents via metadata and file retrieval. The UI will reflect this state (e.g., by disabling search or showing a warning), but no user-facing operation will be blocked. The indexing service will be optional at startup and can be disabled via configuration.

This approach balances the need for efficient fulltext search with the requirement to keep the core system simple, reliable, and resilient. It adheres to the principle of separation of concerns, keeps dependencies minimal, and ensures that document handling remains functional even when search indexing is unavailable or broken.

## Decision: Aggregates must validate business invariants immediately after any state-changing operation, and if an invariant is violated, the aggregate must reject the operation and return a domain-specific error to the client without persisting any changes. Validation is performed synchronously within the aggregate's methods, ensuring that no inconsistent state is ever exposed to the outside world. The aggregate maintains an internal state that is only updated after successful validation, and any attempt to modify state that would violate a business rule results in an immediate halt to processing. The error returned to the client includes a descriptive message and a domain-specific error code, enabling clear communication of the violation without exposing internal implementation details. This approach enforces strong consistency at the aggregate level and prevents the system from entering invalid states. The validation logic is implemented as part of the aggregate's public methods, ensuring that all external interactions are subject to the same invariant checks. No side effects (e.g., events, external calls) are allowed after a validation failure, preserving the integrity of the domain model. This decision aligns with the principles of Domain-Driven Design, where aggregates are the primary enforcement points for business rules, and ensures that the domain remains the single source of truth for consistency.

## Decision: Use a minimal, official base image from the Docker Hub (e.g., `alpine`, `debian:slim`, or `distroless`) tailored to the application’s runtime requirements, prioritizing security, size, and maintainability.

Rationale: Starting from a minimal base image reduces the attack surface by including only essential components, minimizes image size for faster builds and deployments, and lowers the risk of introducing vulnerabilities present in larger or less curated images. Official images from Docker Hub are regularly updated, audited, and maintained by the community and respective project teams, ensuring reliability and compatibility. For example, `alpine` provides a tiny footprint ideal for static binaries, while `distroless` images contain only the application and its runtime dependencies, eliminating unnecessary tools and shells. Using a well-known, supported base image also simplifies dependency management and ensures better compatibility with CI/CD pipelines and orchestration platforms. Avoiding custom or untrusted base images prevents supply chain risks. The choice of base should align with the application’s language and runtime (e.g., `python:3.12-slim` for Python, `golang:1.22-alpine` for Go), balancing performance, security, and resource efficiency. This approach supports reproducible builds, faster pull times, and improved compliance with security best practices.

## Decision: Implement a declarative versioning system for declarations and filters using immutable versioned snapshots with a centralized version registry.

We will implement a versioning mechanism that captures the complete state of declarations and filters at the time a snapshot is taken, ensuring that any historical version can be accurately regenerated regardless of subsequent changes. Each snapshot will be associated with a unique, immutable version identifier and stored alongside a complete, serialized representation of the declaration and filter configuration at that point in time. These snapshots will be managed through a centralized version registry that maintains a version history, including metadata such as timestamp, user, and change description.

To support regeneration, every versioned declaration and filter set will be stored as an immutable artifact, with no mutable state allowed post-creation. The system will enforce this immutability by design, preventing any direct modification of past versions.
