Nginx will be deployed as a reverse proxy in front of Gunicorn to handle static asset delivery, SSL termination, and client request buffering. Static assets (CSS, images, icons, etc.) for the admin pages will be collected into a dedicated directory and served directly by Nginx using a dedicated server block configured to serve static files from the appropriate filesystem path. This separation ensures that Gunicorn is not burdened with serving static content, which improves performance and resource utilization. Nginx will also enforce security best practices by limiting request body sizes, rate-limiting excessive requests, and preventing potential Denial of Service attacks through connection limits and timeouts. Gunicorn will only handle dynamic requests, maintaining a clean separation of concerns. The Nginx configuration will include proper caching headers for static assets to reduce latency and server load. All communication between Nginx and Gunicorn will occur over a local Unix socket for improved performance over TCP. This architecture aligns with production best practices, enhances scalability, and ensures robustness under high load or adversarial conditions.

## Decision: Adopt a scoped, component-level CSS methodology using CSS Modules or similar scoped CSS solution, with strict guidelines against global or shared class reuse.

To mitigate the risks of unintended side effects from CSS modifications in OpenBounty’s web application, we will use CSS Modules (or an equivalent scoped CSS approach) for all new UI components. This ensures that each component’s styles are locally scoped by default, preventing global namespace pollution and eliminating the possibility of one component’s styling inadvertently affecting another. Any class defined within a component’s CSS file will be automatically prefixed with a unique identifier at build time, making it impossible to reference the class from outside the component unless explicitly exported.

We will prohibit the creation of generic, reusable CSS classes (e.g., `.btn`, `.container`, `.text-center`) unless they are part of a formally maintained, versioned design system with strict change control. Even then, such classes will only be used via explicit, documented APIs and will be accompanied by automated regression tests that verify their visual behavior across known use cases.

Additionally, we will enforce a code review policy that requires all CSS changes to be accompanied by a justification for why a new class is needed instead of modifying an existing one, and any modification to a shared or global class must be approved by a design system lead. This ensures that changes to CSS are intentional, traceable, and do not break existing component behavior.

This approach decouples component styling from global state, reduces coupling between UI elements, and makes CSS changes safer and more predictable—aligning with the principles of modern frontend architecture while addressing the inherent brittleness of traditional CSS.

## Decision: Restrict sudo access in Notebook containers by implementing a least-privilege security model using custom, non-root user accounts with explicit, role-based permissions via a dedicated, auditable privilege escalation mechanism.

To mitigate the elevated security risks associated with granting sudo access in Notebook containers—despite improved root isolation in modern Docker—this architecture will prohibit direct root access and instead enforce a strict, auditable privilege escalation workflow. Each notebook container will run as a non-root user with minimal required privileges by default. Administrative actions requiring elevated permissions will be facilitated through a dedicated, sandboxed privilege escalation service (e.g., a lightweight, hardened wrapper around sudo or a custom, policy-driven command executor), which is configured via a centralized, version-controlled policy engine. This service will log all escalation attempts, enforce time-limited sessions, and validate actions against a deny-by-default policy. Access to this escalation mechanism will be restricted to authenticated, authorized users via identity-aware access controls (e.g., OAuth2-integrated with user identity verification), and all operations will be subject to audit logging and real-time monitoring. This approach ensures that even if a container is compromised, the attacker cannot gain persistent or unrestricted root access, and all privileged actions are traceable and reversible. By decoupling privilege escalation from the container runtime and enforcing strict access control, we maintain usability for legitimate administrative tasks while significantly reducing the attack surface and blast radius of potential breaches.

## Decision: Implement a custom MessageConverter that selectively bypasses deserialization for plain text payloads while preserving the default behavior for structured data.

To address the incompatibility between JMS built-in deserializers and plain text payloads, introduce a custom MessageConverter implementation that extends Spring’s `MessageConverter` interface. This converter will inspect the incoming message type and content before attempting deserialization. For messages identified as plain text (e.g., `String` payloads with no structured format), the converter will return the raw payload without invoking any deserialization logic, thereby preventing exceptions. For all other message types (e.g., serialized objects), the converter will delegate to the default JMS deserializer. The decision ensures that plain text messages are handled gracefully and transparently, without requiring changes to the calling classes. The custom converter is registered as the default `MessageConverter` in the JMS configuration, replacing the default implementation. This approach maintains backward compatibility, preserves type safety for structured messages, and provides a clean, extensible solution that can be further enhanced to support additional message types or validation rules. By centralizing the logic in a single, reusable component, the solution improves maintainability and reduces the risk of inconsistent handling across the application.

## Decision

We will retain the current approach of parsing CAPI block elements into a list of `BodyBlock` objects within the frontend model, as it provides a consistent, type-safe, and maintainable abstraction for representing content blocks. This structure is already well-integrated into the liveblog rendering pipeline and has proven effective in handling diverse block types (e.g., text, image, video, quote) with appropriate metadata and rendering logic. By preserving this model, we ensure backward compatibility, reduce the risk of regressions during content transformation, and maintain a clear separation between content parsing and presentation. Additionally, forwarding the `BodyBlock` list to dotcom rendering aligns with our goal of shared content modeling across platforms, enabling consistent rendering and reducing duplication of parsing logic. Any future enhancements to block semantics or new block types will be introduced through incremental extension of the `BodyBlock` interface, with clear versioning and migration paths. This decision avoids the complexity and risk of introducing a new intermediate format or diverging from the established pattern, ensuring long-term maintainability and scalability of the frontend content pipeline.

## Decision: Accept and process the JSON serialization output from Scratch directly, without attempting to convert it to a .sb3 file.

We have decided to accept the JSON-formatted serialization output provided by Scratch as the primary data format for transferring scratch saves to the local web server. This decision is based on the direct availability of a reliable, well-documented function within Scratch that serializes the project state into a structured JSON object, which accurately represents the project's code, assets, and metadata. Rather than implementing or relying on an external method to generate a .sb3 file (which would require additional file system manipulation, ZIP library integration, and potential compatibility issues), we leverage the native JSON output as a first-class format.

The JSON format is sufficient for our use case because it contains all necessary information to reconstruct the project state in the web environment, including blocks, sprites, costumes, sounds, and project properties. By processing this JSON directly, we eliminate the need for intermediate file conversion steps, reducing complexity, improving reliability, and avoiding potential errors introduced by ZIP manipulation or file format translation. Additionally, the JSON format is natively supported by web applications, enabling seamless parsing, validation, and rendering in the browser without additional dependencies.

This approach also aligns with modern web practices, where JSON is the standard for data interchange, and supports future extensibility, such as incremental updates or versioning. While the .sb3 format remains a valid container for Scratch projects, the decision to forgo its use in favor of the native JSON serialization ensures a leaner, more maintainable integration path that prioritizes performance, correctness, and simplicity.

## Decision

Adopt GitHub Actions as the CI/CD solution for managing builds, tests, and deployments to the Kubernetes cluster. Despite familiarity with CircleCI and prior experience with SolanoCI, GitHub Actions is selected due to its tight integration with GitHub repositories, native support for Kubernetes deployments via GitHub Actions Runner or external runners, and a free tier that aligns with the need for cost-effective testing. GitHub Actions offers a syntax and workflow model that closely mirrors CircleCI, minimizing the learning curve and enabling reuse of existing CI/CD knowledge. Additionally, its seamless handling of pull request workflows, artifact management, and environment-specific deployment (via secrets and environments) supports secure and repeatable release processes. The decision avoids the time investment required to set up and maintain external CI systems like Jenkins or GitLab CI, while still providing the flexibility to scale with custom runners and reusable workflows. GitHub Actions’ extensive ecosystem of community actions and first-party support for Kubernetes (e.g., kubectl, Helm, and container image building) ensures robust, maintainable, and future-proof automation. This choice enables rapid implementation without compromising on functionality, security, or scalability.

## Decision

We will name the wrappers using the prefix `MdtpHmrc` followed by a descriptive, camelCase component name that reflects its purpose and origin, e.g., `MdtpHmrcHeader`, `MdtpHmrcFooter`, `MdtpHmrcBanner`, `MdtpHmrcNotificationBadge`, `MdtpHmrcTimeoutDialog`. This naming convention ensures:  
- **Clear lineage and provenance**: The `MdtpHmrc` prefix explicitly identifies the component as a platform-specific wrapper for HMRC-specific Nunjucks components on the MDTP platform.  
- **Consistency with MDTP conventions**: The prefix aligns with existing MDTP naming patterns (e.g., `MdtpComponent`, `MdtpForm`, `MdtpLayout`) and distinguishes platform-level abstractions from raw Nunjucks ports.  
- **Avoiding confusion with GDS components**: It prevents teams from mistaking these wrappers for standard GDS components, which are typically named `Govuk*` (e.g., `GovukHeader`).  
- **Scalability and discoverability**: The pattern allows for predictable naming of future HMRC-specific wrappers, making them easy to locate and understand in codebases.  
- **Semantic clarity**: The suffix (e.g., `Banner`, `NotificationBadge`) clearly communicates the component’s function, while the prefix signals it is a platform-optimized, Play-integrated version of a legacy Nunjucks component.  

This approach ensures that teams use the correct, platform-aware components without needing to understand the underlying Nunjucks implementation or manually wire in language, routing, or accessibility features.

## Decision: Use a dedicated configuration management system with version-controlled JSON schema and transformation scripts stored in a private Git repository, integrated via a CI/CD pipeline to dynamically generate and apply Elasticsearch mappings and data transformations during the import process.

The application requires complex, rich JSON-based configurations for Elasticsearch mappings and data transformations that exceed the capabilities of environment variables. To ensure maintainability, traceability, and consistency across environments, we adopt a configuration-as-code approach using a private Git repository to store all mapping definitions, transformation logic (in JavaScript or Python), and schema validation rules. These artifacts are version-controlled, reviewed via pull requests, and managed with appropriate access controls. A CI/CD pipeline automatically validates the configuration on commit, builds a deployable artifact (e.g., a container image or configuration bundle), and executes the import process in a controlled, idempotent manner. During execution, the pipeline loads the configuration files at runtime, applies the mappings to Elasticsearch, and executes the transformation functions on the raw data prior to indexing. This approach eliminates hard-coded values, supports auditability, enables safe rollbacks, and allows for automated testing of mapping and transformation logic in staging environments before production deployment. It also facilitates collaboration among data engineers, DevOps, and application developers without exposing sensitive logic or requiring environment-specific configuration management.

## Decision: Implement a standardized Architectural Decision Record (ADR) process for all new architectural decisions.

All architectural decisions made during the project lifecycle must be documented using a consistent ADR template. The ADR will include: (1) the context and problem being addressed, (2) the proposed solution, (3) alternatives considered and why they were rejected, (4) the decision made, (5) the consequences of the decision (both positive and negative), and (6) the date and author. ADRs will be stored in a dedicated, version-controlled repository within the project’s documentation system, accessible to all team members. The process will be mandatory for all significant architectural decisions, including but not limited to technology selection, system decomposition, data modeling, integration patterns, and security design. ADRs will be reviewed by a designated architecture review board or peer group prior to finalization to ensure clarity, completeness, and alignment with project goals. Existing undocumented decisions will be retroactively captured where possible through team retrospectives and stakeholder interviews. The ADR process will be enforced via team onboarding, documentation standards, and integration into the project’s development workflow. This ensures that architectural knowledge is preserved, decisions are traceable, and future teams can understand the rationale behind design choices, preventing the loss of institutional knowledge.

## Decision: Implement a continuous vulnerability monitoring and automated dependency update system using Snyk or Dependabot integrated into the CI/CD pipeline.

We will adopt Snyk or Dependabot as our primary tool for continuous monitoring of third-party open source dependencies. These tools will automatically scan the application’s dependency tree (including transitive dependencies) against a maintained vulnerability database (e.g., NVD, Snyk’s own database) on every code commit and pull request. When a known vulnerability is detected, the system will generate a security alert with severity rating, affected versions, and remediation guidance.

To ensure timely response, we will configure the system to enforce security policy checks within the CI/CD pipeline. Any pull request introducing a high or critical severity vulnerability will block merging until the dependency is updated or the risk is explicitly approved via a documented exception process. The system will generate automated pull requests for dependency updates, including upgrades to secure versions, with minimal manual intervention required.

We will also maintain a centralized dependency inventory and a documented process for reviewing and approving dependency updates, including impact analysis for breaking changes. Security alerts will be routed to a dedicated team via Slack or email, with escalation paths for unresolved issues. Regular vulnerability scanning reports will be generated and reviewed during security audits.

This approach ensures proactive detection of vulnerabilities, rapid response through automation, and enforceable security hygiene across all development environments. It reduces the risk of introducing known vulnerabilities and enables the team to maintain a secure, up-to-date dependency ecosystem with minimal operational overhead.

## Decision: Use AWS Cognito for user authentication and token generation

Adopt AWS Cognito as the identity and access management solution to enable user authentication via third-party providers (GitHub, Google, etc.) and issue secure tokens for API access. Cognito will manage user pools for storing user identities, support federated sign-in through OAuth 2.0 with OpenID Connect, and issue JWT tokens that are validated by the API Gateway. These tokens will carry claims that identify the user and their associated data pool, enabling the backend to securely isolate and retrieve each user’s data from DynamoDB. Cognito integrates natively with API Gateway, allowing the API key and usage plan to coexist with token-based authorization, where the token is checked after the API key. This approach eliminates the need to manage user credentials or authentication state in the backend, reduces attack surface, and supports scalable, secure multi-tenant data isolation. The use of Cognito also future-proofs the system for features like multi-factor authentication, password recovery, and user management via the Cognito Admin APIs. While Cognito introduces some complexity in configuration and domain management, its deep integration with AWS services, built-in support for identity federation, and compliance with industry standards make it the optimal choice for implementing secure, scalable user authentication and data isolation in this architecture.

## Decision

The Endpoint resource shall be governed by a dual-control architecture where the Endpoint Reconciler is responsible for maintaining the desired state of the Endpoint resource by reconciling its specification against the actual state, ensuring consistency with the intended configuration. The Prober (via ProbeManager and associated Workers) operates independently to actively monitor the health and reachability of endpoints by executing periodic probes. The Prober is not responsible for state reconciliation but instead reports observed conditions (e.g., connectivity, latency, failure) back to the Endpoint resource as status updates. The Reconciler remains the authoritative source for desired state, while the Prober provides observational feedback that informs the Reconciler’s decisions through status fields, but does not override or dictate the desired state. This separation ensures that control logic remains decoupled: the Reconciler focuses on configuration consistency and lifecycle management, while the Prober focuses on runtime observability and failure detection. The Prober’s results are used to enrich the Endpoint’s status, including conditions like `Ready`, `Unreachable`, or `Degraded`, which the Reconciler may consider during reconciliation cycles, but the Reconciler retains final authority over state transitions. This design prevents conflicting state mutations, reduces complexity in the reconciliation loop, and enables scalable, resilient endpoint monitoring without compromising the integrity of the desired state.

## Decision

Each component story in Storybook shall be implemented with a standardized structure that includes interactive knobs for all configurable properties, organized into logical groups, and enriched with comprehensive documentation via the notes tab. Knobs shall be defined for every public property of the component, enabling real-time interaction and visualization of variations. Mandatory properties shall be grouped under a dedicated "Mandatory" section, while optional properties shall be grouped under "Optional," ensuring clear separation of required and non-required inputs. Additional groups such as "Use Cases" and "States" may be included only when necessary to demonstrate specific scenarios or edge cases. All knob values shall be derived from the component’s documented API, with appropriate types and defaults to ensure consistency and usability. The notes tab shall contain a JSON-formatted data object representing the component’s expected input, including all relevant properties and their values, and shall also include a Twig include code example for direct use in templates. This JSON object shall be generated programmatically from the story’s default parameters and validated to match the component’s schema, ensuring accuracy and reducing manual errors. This approach ensures that stories are not only interactive and visually informative but also serve as a reliable source of truth for both developers and designers, facilitating consistent implementation across the codebase.

## Decision: Retain and Replatform Salesforce as the Primary CRM System with a Phased Data and Configuration Cleanup

Given that Salesforce was originally designed as a CRM platform and has already been adopted within CCS for commercial agreement management, it is the most viable and strategic choice to implement as the organisation’s primary CRM system. Retaining Salesforce ensures continuity of investment, leverages existing user familiarity, and avoids the risks and costs associated with adopting a new CRM platform. However, due to the significant customisations and poor-quality data in the existing instance, a comprehensive replatforming strategy is mandated.

The decision is to retain the Salesforce instance but treat it as a new CRM deployment, not a continuation of the legacy system. This involves a full data cleanse, removal of legacy customisations that do not align with modern CRM best practices, and a re-architected data model focused on CRM use cases (e.g., accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities, campaigns). A phased migration approach will be adopted: first, a clean data foundation will be established using data governance and deduplication tools; second, core CRM functionality will be rebuilt using standard Salesforce features and approved customisations; third, integration with existing CCS processes will be re-established through modern APIs and middleware.

This approach balances business continuity with long-term maintainability and scalability. It avoids the technical debt of maintaining a legacy system while preserving the strategic advantage of using a mature, extensible CRM platform. The project will include a dedicated data quality initiative, change management, and training to ensure adoption and data integrity. The outcome will be a modern, performant, and sustainable CRM system built on Salesforce, aligned with the organisation’s strategic objectives.

## Decision

Styles for React components should be defined in the same file as the component, located above the component definition. This approach is preferred because it reduces cognitive overhead and development friction by eliminating the need to navigate between files for related logic and styling. The simplicity of keeping styles colocated with their component ensures faster onboarding, easier refactoring, and better maintainability for small to medium-sized components. While larger files may become harder to read, modern IDEs provide robust code folding capabilities that mitigate this concern effectively. The reduction in file count also decreases the burden on Babel transformation and file watchers, improving build and development performance. The minor additional effort of managing styles within the component file is outweighed by the benefits of consistency, locality, and reduced complexity. This decision aligns with the prevailing patterns in the React ecosystem, particularly with tools like styled-components and CSS-in-JS libraries that emphasize colocated styling. Therefore, all React components should have their styles defined in the same file, above the component, unless there is a compelling reason to extract them (e.g., shared styles across multiple components).

## Decision

Adopt a monorepo structure using a single Git repository to manage all related codebases, including the main application, shared libraries, testing utilities, and documentation. This decision is grounded in the principle of using familiar tools and aligning with industry best practices for maintainability, consistency, and developer experience. The monorepo will be managed with a modern build and dependency management system such as Nx or Turborepo, which provide efficient incremental builds, deterministic dependency resolution, and robust tooling for code generation, linting, testing, and deployment. All projects within the monorepo will follow a consistent directory structure and naming convention to ensure clarity and ease of navigation. Versioning will be handled via a centralized versioning strategy (e.g., semantic versioning with automated changelog generation), using tools like conventional commits and release scripts to maintain consistency across packages. Access control and branch protection policies will be enforced at the repository level, with pull request workflows requiring peer review, passing CI checks, and adherence to contribution guidelines. The monorepo will be supported by a shared configuration system for linters, formatters, and test runners to ensure uniform code quality across all projects. This approach enables faster iteration, reduces duplication, simplifies cross-project refactoring, and enhances collaboration, while still allowing individual packages to be published independently when needed. The decision to use a monorepo is justified by its proven success in large-scale software systems, its compatibility with familiar developer workflows, and its alignment with the team’s preference for simplicity, transparency, and maintainability.

## Decision

The module shall not enforce or assume the presence of a DNS hosted zone in AWS, nor shall it require direct access to AWS Route 53 or any other DNS service. Instead, the module will support configuration via user-provided DNS records, allowing users to manage DNS resolution externally through any DNS provider or in a separate AWS account. The module will accept DNS-related inputs such as domain names, record values, and endpoint addresses as explicit parameters, enabling users to define the necessary DNS configuration in their own infrastructure or via external tools. This design ensures compatibility with cross-account, multi-account, or hybrid cloud environments where direct access to the hosted zone is restricted or unavailable. By decoupling DNS management from the module’s deployment logic, the solution remains flexible, secure, and aligned with least-privilege access patterns. The module will document clear instructions for users to configure DNS records manually or via their preferred automation method, ensuring reliable service discovery without dependency on AWS DNS resources. This approach supports compliance with security policies, reduces attack surface by avoiding unnecessary IAM permissions, and enables broader adoption across diverse deployment models.

## Decision

Files shall be formatted programmatically using a dedicated `format.js` script that invokes standardized formatting tools (e.g., Prettier, ESLint, or similar). This approach ensures consistent formatting across all development environments regardless of IDE, editor, or local configuration. The script will be integrated into the project's `package.json` as a top-level command (e.g., `npm run format`) and can be executed manually or automatically via pre-commit hooks using `lint-staged`. This eliminates reliance on developer-specific IDE plugins, which vary in installation, configuration, and usage, and avoids inconsistencies caused by unformatted or improperly formatted files. Additionally, the script enables centralized control over formatting rules, making it easier to enforce code style standards uniformly across the team. By treating formatting as a deterministic, repeatable process, the team reduces friction during code reviews and ensures that all code entering the repository meets the defined formatting standards. This solution is scalable, maintainable, and aligns with industry best practices for code quality and consistency.

## Decision

All incoming requests to the backend server shall be validated using a standardized, schema-driven validation framework that enforces the same validation rules as those implemented on the mobile and front-end applications. The validation will be applied at the entry point of each API endpoint, prior to any business logic execution, using a shared validation schema definition (e.g., JSON Schema or similar) that is versioned and maintained in a centralized repository accessible to both the backend and front-end teams. This ensures consistency across platforms and eliminates discrepancies in validation behavior. Validation errors will be returned in a uniform, machine-readable format (e.g., JSON with structured error messages including field names, error codes, and descriptive messages) to enable the front-end and mobile clients to handle them predictably and display meaningful feedback when required. The validation framework will support both synchronous and asynchronous request handling, with validation occurring synchronously during request processing to prevent invalid data from progressing through the system. Additionally, the backend will reject requests with incomplete or invalid data immediately, returning a 400 Bad Request HTTP status code with a detailed error payload. This approach ensures robustness, consistency, and seamless integration with the asynchronous nature of the front-end, while minimizing the risk of data corruption or unintended side effects due to malformed input.

## Decision: User code must explicitly configure and propagate distributed tracing context via standardized headers and metadata, leveraging Dapr’s injected correlation ID as the root trace identifier. Dapr will continue to inject a unique correlation ID into HTTP headers (e.g., `dapr-trace-id`) and gRPC metadata (e.g., `dapr-trace-id`) at the ingress boundary, ensuring end-to-end traceability across service boundaries. However, Dapr will not enforce or provide built-in tracing instrumentation, such as sampling, span creation, or export to tracing backends (e.g., OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, or Zipkin). Instead, user code is responsible for: (1) extracting the correlation ID from incoming requests; (2) initializing tracing spans using the correlation ID as the parent context; (3) propagating the trace context via outgoing HTTP headers or gRPC metadata; and (4) exporting spans to a tracing backend. This approach preserves Dapr’s minimal operational footprint, avoids vendor lock-in, and allows users to select their preferred tracing implementation. Dapr will provide documented conventions for header and metadata naming, trace context propagation formats (e.g., W3C Trace Context), and examples in multiple languages to guide users. The decision ensures compatibility with industry standards while maintaining flexibility for users to adopt tracing solutions that match their infrastructure, compliance, and observability requirements.

## Decision

We have decided to adopt **Algolia** as the primary search solution for this project. Algolia meets all the required functionality criteria—flexible facet management, synonym configuration, query suggestions, configurable misspelling tolerance, natural language query support, and integration with external data sources—out of the box with minimal configuration overhead. Its intuitive UI enables non-technical stakeholders to manage and refine search behavior independently, reducing dependency on development resources. The platform’s robust API, real-time indexing, and prebuilt frontend components significantly accelerate implementation and iteration cycles, aligning well with agile delivery expectations. While Bloomreach Search & Merchandising (brSM) shows promise and is being evaluated in a POC, its current focus on e-commerce and merchandising workflows introduces unnecessary complexity and potential misalignment with NHS Digital’s content-centric use case. Native Lucene search lacks essential features such as synonym management and natural language understanding, rendering it unsuitable for advanced search requirements. Azure Cognitive Search and Amazon Kendra/Elasticsearch offer strong capabilities but require greater operational overhead, infrastructure management, and customization effort, which would delay time-to-market and increase long-term maintenance burden. Algolia’s proven track record in high-availability, low-latency search experiences, combined with its developer-friendly ecosystem and strong support for content-driven applications, makes it the optimal choice for delivering a performant, maintainable, and extensible search solution that meets both current and future requirements.

## Decision: Integrate JSDOM as the primary HTML parsing library for unit tests and content manipulation

Adopt JSDOM as the standard HTML parsing and manipulation library for the project, particularly for use in unit tests and content transformation utilities such as `transform.js`. JSDOM provides a robust, mature, and widely adopted DOM implementation that fully supports HTML parsing, traversal, and manipulation, including essential properties and methods like `innerHTML`, `textContent`, `querySelector`, and `addEventListener`. This capability directly addresses the limitations of the bundled XML parser, which, despite being able to parse HTML, lacks basic DOM-level operations required for effective content assertions and transformations in test scenarios.

JSDOM’s API closely mirrors browser behavior, enabling consistent and reliable test execution across environments. Its support for modern HTML and CSS standards ensures compatibility with real-world content, while its ability to create isolated document contexts allows for safe, side-effect-free testing. The library is well-maintained, has extensive documentation, and is widely used in the JavaScript ecosystem, minimizing risk and ensuring long-term sustainability.

By integrating JSDOM, the team gains the ability to write expressive, readable, and maintainable unit tests that assert on rendered HTML structure and behavior, significantly improving test quality and developer productivity. The decision to use JSDOM is not limited to test environments—its utility extends to any scenario requiring programmatic HTML manipulation, such as server-side rendering validation or content transformation pipelines. The performance overhead is acceptable given the critical role of testing and content integrity in the application.

## Decision: Establish a centralized, policy-driven GitHub Organization Assignment Framework

To ensure consistent and secure allocation of source repositories to the correct GitHub organizations, we will implement a centralized policy-driven framework that determines organization assignment based on predefined, auditable criteria. The framework will be governed by a set of rules encoded in infrastructure-as-code (IaC) using a configuration management system (e.g., Terraform or GitHub Enterprise Cloud policies), with enforcement via automated checks in CI/CD pipelines and repository creation workflows.

The assignment rules will be based on the following factors, in order of precedence: (1) project ownership and team affiliation (mapped to defined organizational units), (2) data classification and compliance requirements (e.g., PII, regulatory data), (3) technical environment (e.g., production, staging, research), and (4) historical patterns and domain-specific naming conventions. Each repository creation request—whether via API, CLI, or UI—must pass through a pre-defined validation step that evaluates these criteria and resolves the target organization.

The decision logic will be version-controlled, reviewed through pull requests, and auditable via change logs and audit trails. Access to modify the assignment rules will be restricted to a designated governance team with defined roles and approval workflows. Additionally, a governance dashboard will provide visibility into repository placement, compliance status, and drift detection.

This approach ensures consistency, minimizes human error, supports compliance, and enables scalability as the number of teams and repositories grows. It also prevents accidental creation of repositories in incorrect or unapproved organizations, reducing security and governance risks.

## Decision
Adopt a single, standardized base image across all container images—specifically, Debian Slim (buster-slim or bullseye-slim)—to ensure consistency, reduce image size, improve security, and simplify maintenance. Debian Slim provides a minimal footprint while offering broad compatibility with common system libraries, package management (apt), and well-documented behavior. This choice eliminates the variability introduced by using multiple base images (e.g., Fedora and Alpine), which differ in package formats, library versions, and system behaviors, reducing the risk of runtime inconsistencies, dependency conflicts, and security vulnerabilities. Additionally, Debian Slim’s long-term support (LTS) and active community ensure reliable updates and vulnerability patching. All new container images will use Debian Slim as the default base, and existing images will be migrated incrementally during routine updates. This standardization enables streamlined CI/CD pipelines, simplified image scanning, and improved developer onboarding by providing a predictable, well-understood foundation.

## Decision: Migrate from plain JavaScript to AngularJS

We decided to migrate the project from plain JavaScript to AngularJS to leverage the benefits of a modern frontend framework. The existing implementation, while functional, lacked modularity, maintainability, and reusability—key challenges in scaling the application. AngularJS offers a structured approach to building dynamic web applications through two-way data binding, dependency injection, directives, and a clear separation of concerns between the view, logic, and data.

The decision was driven by the need to improve code organization, reduce boilerplate, and enhance developer productivity. AngularJS’s declarative syntax simplifies the manipulation of the DOM and state management, reducing the likelihood of errors in event handling and data synchronization. Additionally, AngularJS’s support for reusable components (via custom directives and services) aligns with the project’s evolving feature set, enabling the team to build and maintain features more efficiently.

Although SoundCloud’s JavaScript SDK remained a third-party dependency, AngularJS provided a clean integration layer, allowing us to encapsulate SDK interactions within services and maintain separation of concerns. The framework’s built-in testing tools and support for unit and end-to-end testing also improved the project’s long-term maintainability and reliability.

While AngularJS introduces a learning curve and additional runtime overhead, the trade-off is justified by the significant gains in code quality, scalability, and developer experience. This migration positions the application for future growth and paves the way for adopting more advanced patterns and tools as the project evolves.

## Decision: Expose ETL output via a RESTful API gateway hosted within the same Kubernetes namespace as the ETL container, using a dedicated microservice with a stateless design and role-based access control (RBAC). The microservice will poll the ETL container’s output directory at configurable intervals, validate data integrity using checksums, and serve the data through a versioned JSON endpoint. All requests will be authenticated via JWT tokens issued by an integrated OAuth2 provider, with rate limiting enforced at the gateway level. Data will be cached in-memory for up to 5 minutes to reduce latency and avoid redundant file reads, with cache invalidation triggered on new ETL output or manual refresh. The API will support pagination, filtering, and schema versioning to ensure backward compatibility. Monitoring and logging will be implemented using structured JSON logs and integrated with the centralized observability stack (Prometheus + Grafana + ELK), with health checks exposed on a dedicated /health endpoint. This approach ensures secure, performant, and reliable access to ETL output while decoupling the data production from consumption layers, enabling independent scaling and lifecycle management of both components.

## Decision

Adopt DfE Sign-in (DSI) as the authentication provider for the service, despite the service not requiring access to school or user data held within DSI. The decision is based on DfE governance approval and the need to align with established DfE identity standards, ensuring consistent trust and compliance across government services. Although the service does not require user or school data, DSI’s implementation of modern, open standards—specifically OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC)—provides a secure, password-less authentication mechanism that meets the service’s security and usability requirements. DSI’s use of standardized protocols ensures interoperability, auditability, and resistance to common authentication threats such as phishing and credential theft. By leveraging DSI, the service benefits from centralized identity management, improved audit trails, and reduced risk of identity-related vulnerabilities. The absence of a formal tool recommendation in the technical guidance does not preclude the use of DSI, as it remains the approved identity provider for DfE services. Furthermore, DSI’s integration with multi-factor authentication (MFA) and its support for secure session management align with modern security best practices. The decision to use DSI ensures the service maintains a consistent, trusted, and auditable authentication flow while enabling secure access for authorized school buying professionals, with all public access restricted appropriately through role-based access control (RBAC) and proper scope management. This approach balances security, compliance, and operational simplicity without introducing unnecessary complexity or proprietary solutions.

## Decision: Adopt Sass with the `sass` implementation (Dart Sass) for centralized CSS variable management and advanced styling capabilities.

Sass is selected as the preferred solution for managing shared CSS variables and enabling advanced styling features across the application. The decision is based on several key factors: Sass provides native support for variables, nesting, mixins, and partials—essential for creating a scalable and maintainable style system—while ensuring consistent behavior across development and build environments. The `sass` implementation (Dart Sass) is chosen over `node-sass` due to its faster performance, better integration with modern build tools, and more reliable dependency management, as it does not rely on native compilation or external C libraries. Additionally, Dart Sass is actively maintained, has excellent TypeScript support, and is the official recommended implementation by the Sass team.

While PostCSS offers flexibility through plugins, it requires additional configuration and plugin management (e.g., `postcss-sass`, `postcss-nested`, `autoprefixer`) to replicate Sass’s out-of-the-box functionality, increasing complexity and potential for configuration drift. In contrast, Sass provides a unified, opinionated, and well-documented approach to writing modular, reusable CSS. By using Sass with `sass`, we can define a central `variables.scss` and `mixins.scss` file that are imported by component-level CSS modules, enabling consistent application-wide styling without duplication.

This decision aligns with ADR # 8, ensuring that component-scoped CSS remains isolated while allowing access to shared design tokens. The use of Sass also future-proofs the codebase for advanced features like responsive utilities, theming, and dynamic styling, while maintaining compatibility with existing CSS module workflows.

## Decision

We will revise the cell provisioning policy to reduce the number of active cells by 40%, transitioning from a conservative over-provisioning model to a more capacity-efficient configuration while maintaining resilience and operational safety. This decision is based on empirical data showing consistent underutilization of memory (77–92% usable), low container utilization (10% average, peaking at 20% above prior week), and minimal CPU contention (10% average, 80% peak). The historical rationale in ADR017—driven by high per-tenant quotas and limited tenant count—no longer reflects current conditions, where individual tenant memory demands are a small fraction of total cell capacity. Given that cells remain distributed across three AZs and the risk of capacity exhaustion remains low, we can safely reduce the total cell count without compromising availability. We will implement a phased reduction over 6 weeks, monitoring memory pressure, container scheduling success, and memory allocation trends weekly. A safety threshold will be enforced: if usable memory drops below 70% or container scheduling fails due to memory constraints, the reduction will pause and revert. This revised policy will be reviewed quarterly, with the option to further adjust based on observed usage patterns. The change will reduce infrastructure costs while preserving the ability to absorb sudden demand spikes, particularly given the 55% week-on-week memory increase observed in the largest tenant.

## Decision

We will modify the Processor to enforce explicit program termination via an exit system call by introducing a bounded Address space with a well-defined maximum limit, and by treating any attempt to execute beyond this limit as a program termination error. The Processor will now maintain a fixed-size Address space (e.g., 65,536 addresses) and validate all instruction fetches against this bound. If the Program counter (PC) reaches the maximum address and the next instruction would require fetching from an address beyond this limit, the Processor will raise a runtime error indicating that the program did not terminate properly via an explicit exit system call. This error will halt execution and return a non-zero exit status, ensuring that programs must explicitly invoke an exit instruction to terminate cleanly. The memory model will be updated to enforce this bound at the hardware level, and the instruction set will include a dedicated `exit` system call that sets a termination flag and returns control to the operating system. This change ensures deterministic and transparent program termination, eliminates ambiguity about whether a program has properly exited, and aligns with the goal of requiring explicit exit behavior for all programs. The bounded Address space also enables the Processor to detect missing exit instructions as a runtime fault, providing a clear signal when a program fails to terminate correctly.

## Decision: Adopt a consistent, version-controlled formatting standard for all katas using a project-wide .editorconfig file and automated code formatting tools (e.g., Prettier or ESLint with auto-fix). The formatting rules will be defined once, documented in the project's README, and enforced via pre-commit hooks. This ensures uniformity across all katas regardless of individual contributor style, eliminates subjective formatting debates, and supports long-term maintainability. Existing katas will be formatted on first major update or when actively modified, with no retroactive formatting of unchanged files. The standard will be reviewed only during major project restructurings or when a widely adopted community standard emerges. This decision prioritizes consistency, scalability, and minimal maintenance overhead over perfect historical formatting alignment.

## Decision: The root-level source directories shall be organized into three top-level modules: `domain`, `application`, and `infrastructure`, with each representing a distinct architectural layer. The `domain` directory contains all core business concepts, entities, and rules, independent of any specific feature or application. The `application` directory contains use cases and features, each implemented as a separate module or subdirectory, with dependencies flowing only from `application` to `domain` and `infrastructure`. The `infrastructure` directory contains adapters, external integrations, and implementation details such as web endpoints, databases, and messaging systems, with no direct dependencies from `application` to `infrastructure` — instead, interfaces defined in `application` are implemented in `infrastructure`. Plugins are implemented as separate modules within the `application` layer, each providing a set of features that can be composed at build time. This structure enforces the dependency rule of Clean Architecture, enables reuse across multiple applications, supports screaming architecture by making feature boundaries explicit in the source tree, and allows for a single-repository development workflow while preserving the integrity of domain and infrastructure separation.

## Decision

We will use Ruby on Rails as the primary framework for developing all new user-facing web applications within GDS. This decision is based on Rails’ strong alignment with the security, consistency, and maintainability requirements for GOV.UK-style applications. Rails provides secure defaults out of the box—such as automatic escaping of user input, protection against common web vulnerabilities (e.g., XSS, CSRF), and robust session management—significantly reducing the risk of introducing security flaws like the XSS vulnerability previously encountered with Sinatra. Its widespread adoption across GDS projects, including the core www.gov.uk platform and the Verify frontend, ensures broad team familiarity and reduces onboarding time for new developers. Furthermore, Rails is the officially supported framework for both the `govuk_template` and `govuk_frontend_toolkit` projects, which provide essential styling, components, and accessibility features. With the upcoming `govuk-frontend` project also expected to maintain Rails compatibility, this choice ensures long-term sustainability and alignment with GDS’s frontend ecosystem. The framework’s maturity, extensive documentation, and active community support make it the most suitable option for delivering consistent, secure, and maintainable user-facing applications across GDS.

## Decision

We will adopt **Styled Components** as our primary CSS-in-JS solution for styling components. This decision is based on its maturity, strong ecosystem, excellent developer experience, and broad community adoption. Styled Components supports both object syntax and tagged template literals (TTL), offering flexibility in how styles are authored while maintaining a clean separation between logic and presentation. The TTL syntax closely resembles standard CSS, enabling developers to write styles in a familiar way with full access to JavaScript expressions, dynamic styling, and scoped styles without global namespace pollution. Additionally, Styled Components integrates seamlessly with React and provides built-in support for server-side rendering, media queries, and pseudo-selectors through a consistent API. While alternatives like CSS Blocks and Stylable offer compelling features, their reliance on custom syntax and pre-processing introduces additional cognitive overhead and tooling complexity, especially for teams with mixed frontend expertise. CSS-in-JS with Styled Components strikes the optimal balance between developer ergonomics, maintainability, and scalability, enabling consistent, reusable, and performant component styling across the codebase.

## Decision

We will continue to update the popularity field in Rummager's search indexes in-place without using index locks, as established in ADR 003. This approach eliminates the need for exclusive locks during bulk updates, allowing the index to remain available for search queries throughout the update process. Instead of creating a new index and atomically switching it in, we perform incremental updates directly to the existing index using a batched, transactional update mechanism that ensures consistency and minimizes performance impact. This decision is justified by the need for high availability of the search service, as locking the entire index for the duration of a bulk load (which could take several minutes) would result in unavailability during critical periods. By updating in-place with careful handling of document versioning and concurrency (e.g., using optimistic concurrency control and idempotent operations), we maintain data integrity while avoiding downtime. The nightly popularity update, which affects every document, is now implemented as a series of small, atomic updates processed in parallel across shards, with progress tracked via a durable state store. This design enables safe, scalable, and performant updates without sacrificing availability, and it aligns with our broader architectural principle of minimizing disruptive maintenance operations. Any future changes to the popularity update process must preserve this in-place, lock-free model unless a compelling alternative is proven to offer equivalent or superior availability and consistency guarantees.

## Decision

We will implement a stateless authentication system using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) issued via a dedicated authentication service, with token validation performed by the frontend service at runtime. The authentication service will be publicly accessible over HTTPS and expose a `/login` endpoint that accepts user credentials and returns a signed JWT containing minimal user claims (e.g., user ID, role, and expiration). The frontend service will store the JWT in an HTTP-only, secure cookie (with SameSite=Strict) to prevent XSS exposure, while also maintaining a local in-memory session state for immediate access to user context. The JWT will be signed using HMAC-SHA256 with a cryptographically strong secret stored in a secure secrets manager and rotated regularly. Token validation will occur on every request to protected routes by the frontend service, which will verify the signature, expiration, and issuer. The authentication service will enforce rate limiting and account lockout after failed attempts to prevent brute-force attacks. This approach ensures secure, scalable, and stateless authentication with minimal server-side session storage, supports public access while protecting sensitive data, and enables seamless integration with modern frontend frameworks.

## Decision: Adopt Cypress as the primary end-to-end testing framework for automated user journey testing across all MOJ applications.

Cypress is selected over Selenium due to its superior developer experience, real-time debugging capabilities, and native support for modern web application patterns. Unlike Selenium, which operates as an external tool controlling a browser remotely, Cypress runs directly within the browser environment, enabling faster test execution, more reliable test results, and better handling of asynchronous operations. This reduces flakiness and improves test stability—critical for maintaining confidence in automated regression suites.

Cypress provides a built-in test runner with live reload, time travel debugging, and detailed command logs, significantly reducing the time required to diagnose and fix failing tests. Its architecture eliminates the need for complex setup, polling, or waiting mechanisms common in Selenium, leading to more maintainable and readable test code. Additionally, Cypress supports modern JavaScript features natively, integrates seamlessly with popular CI/CD pipelines, and offers robust support for mocking APIs and managing test data.

Given that Cypress is already in use across multiple MOJ projects and has proven effective in production environments, adopting it consistently ensures shared knowledge, standardized practices, and reduced onboarding time for new developers. The decision includes establishing a centralized testing library and configuration standards to promote reusability and consistency across teams.

While Selenium remains a viable option for legacy systems or specific browser compatibility requirements, Cypress is designated as the default and preferred framework for all new end-to-end testing initiatives. This decision enables faster feedback loops, improved test reliability, and long-term maintainability of the automated testing suite.

## Decision: Replace the services link with a direct navigation path from the Organisation name in search results to the PIMS Profile Overview page.

The decision to remove the services link from the results page and instead enable navigation to the PIMS Profile Overview page via a clickable Organisation name in the search results is based on improving user experience and streamlining access to core profile information. By making the Organisation name a direct link, users can quickly access the full PIMS Profile Overview without additional navigation steps or intermediary pages. This change reduces cognitive load, eliminates redundant interactions, and aligns with user expectations for immediate access to organizational details after a search. The Organisation name is already a prominent element in the results, making it a natural and discoverable anchor for navigation. This approach also supports consistency with modern UX patterns that emphasize direct, context-aware navigation. The PIMS Profile Overview page contains the most relevant and frequently accessed information about an organisation, including key identifiers, status, and high-level attributes, making it the logical destination for users after a search. This decision enhances usability, particularly for power users and administrators who require rapid access to profile data. It also simplifies the interface by removing a redundant link, reducing visual clutter and improving focus on primary actions. The change is backward compatible with existing workflows and does not impact data integrity or system performance. Implementation is straightforward, requiring only a change in the results rendering logic to make the Organisation name a navigational link to the PIMS Profile Overview page. This decision is aligned with the broader goal of creating a more intuitive, efficient, and user-centered search experience.

## Decision

Adopt a consistent, semantic URL schema based on resource nouns and standardized HTTP verbs, using a REST-inspired pattern with plural resource names and clear, hierarchical paths (e.g., `/donations/new`, `/memberships/apply`, `/contact`). This approach ensures predictability, maintainability, and clarity across the application, reducing cognitive load for developers and improving long-term code quality. The decision to prioritize consistency over SEO is justified by the application’s traffic sources—primarily banner-driven and not content-focused—making the immediate benefit of SEO-optimized URLs negligible. The new schema will be implemented incrementally during feature development, with legacy routes deprecated and redirected to their canonical equivalents. This avoids large-scale refactoring while ensuring all new endpoints follow the new standard. The chosen pattern supports future extensibility, such as API versioning or enhanced routing logic, without requiring architectural changes.

## Decision

We will rebuild the PaaS product pages using Next.js, leveraging its static site generation capabilities with `next export` to produce server-rendered, performant HTML pages. This decision is based on the requirement for non-developers to update content with minimal friction, as Next.js offers a more accessible developer experience compared to Gatsby, which requires a developer environment to install and run. By using Markdown with MDX, we enable structured, human-readable content that supports embedded React components, allowing for rich page layouts while maintaining simplicity for content authors. Next.js’s built-in support for server-side rendering, static generation, and incremental static regeneration aligns with our need for fast, reliable page delivery. Additionally, adopting Next.js ensures technological consistency across our user-facing applications, facilitating shared component libraries and reducing cognitive load for developers. The decision supports long-term maintainability, easier alignment with GOV.UK Design System updates, and improved developer experience across the team.

## Decision

Replace all instances of the Legacy Trackable Interface with the new CoreTrackable Interface across the codebase to ensure consistency, maintainability, and alignment with the updated event tracking architecture. The CoreTrackable Interface provides a standardized, extensible, and type-safe contract for tracking events, including built-in support for metadata, event context, and standardized event emission patterns. Migrating to CoreTrackable eliminates redundancy, reduces the risk of inconsistent tracking implementations, and simplifies future enhancements such as telemetry aggregation, analytics integration, and observability tooling. The migration will be performed incrementally, with automated refactoring tools used where possible, and accompanied by comprehensive unit and integration tests to validate behavior preservation. Legacy Trackable will be deprecated and marked as obsolete, with a clear deprecation notice and migration guide provided in documentation. Any new tracking logic must use CoreTrackable exclusively, and existing code using Legacy Trackable will be phased out within a defined timeline (e.g., 3 months). This decision ensures long-term architectural coherence, reduces technical debt, and enables scalable event tracking across services and platforms.

## Decision: Split the Content Performance Manager and Content Audit Tool into separate repositories and independent codebases.

Given the evolving understanding of user needs, the Content Performance Manager and Content Audit Tool have diverged significantly in purpose, functionality, and target users. While initially grouped together to enable rapid iteration and shared development, user research and usage patterns now reveal distinct workflows: the Content Performance Manager focuses on post-publishing analytics, performance tracking, and optimization recommendations, whereas the Content Audit Tool is centered on pre-publishing quality checks, compliance validation, and editorial consistency.

Maintaining both tools in a single repository has introduced technical and organizational friction—difficulties in prioritization, conflicting release cycles, and unclear ownership—despite initial assumptions of shared requirements. The decision to split is now justified by the principle of separation of concerns: each tool serves a different phase of the content lifecycle and requires independent feature development, testing, and deployment strategies.

Splitting the repositories will enable dedicated ownership, clearer roadmaps, and improved maintainability. It also aligns with best practices in microservices and modular architecture, where tools with distinct responsibilities are managed independently. The separation will not hinder collaboration—shared design systems, documentation, and cross-tool integrations can still be maintained—but it will provide the necessary autonomy to scale each tool effectively.

The decision to split is irreversible at this stage; attempting to merge them again would require significant rework. Therefore, we commit to splitting both applications into separate repositories, with distinct CI/CD pipelines, versioning, and stakeholder teams, effective immediately.

## Decision: Move API request authentication and parameter validation from client-side proxy middleware to server-side API gateway

We decided to refactor the application architecture by removing the client-side proxy middleware and instead implement a server-side API gateway that handles all API request authentication, token validation, and dynamic parameter enforcement. The gateway will authenticate requests using the user's Google token, extract the user's authorized services from the token, and enforce service-level filtering at the gateway layer before forwarding requests to the Evidence API. This change eliminates the ability for clients to tamper with filter parameters, ensuring that only services the user is authorized to access can be requested. Additionally, by centralizing request handling on the server, we can decouple the client from the complexity of managing tokens and authentication, improving both security and maintainability. To mitigate the UX impact of loading states, we will implement a caching layer at the gateway and introduce progressive loading patterns (e.g., skeleton screens, optimistic UI updates) to improve perceived performance. This architectural shift enables tamper-proof API requests, enforces strict access control, and aligns with secure API design best practices while maintaining a responsive user experience.

## Decision: HTML documents shall not rely on `meta` tags for automatic page refreshes or redirects. Instead, client-side JavaScript shall be used to handle dynamic navigation and refresh logic. This decision ensures predictable behavior, improves accessibility, supports progressive enhancement, and aligns with modern web standards. Using `meta` refresh or redirect tags can lead to poor user experience, especially when users are unaware of the automatic change, and may interfere with browser navigation features such as back/forward buttons. JavaScript provides greater control, allows for conditional logic (e.g., only redirect after a delay or based on user state), and enables graceful fallbacks. Furthermore, JavaScript-based navigation integrates better with single-page application (SPA) patterns and can be instrumented for analytics and error tracking. While `meta` tags remain technically valid, their use is discouraged in favor of more robust, maintainable, and user-friendly alternatives. Any necessary refresh or redirect functionality must be implemented via JavaScript, with appropriate user feedback (e.g., loading indicators or confirmation messages) where applicable. This approach enhances maintainability, debugging, and overall application reliability.

## Decision

Use forward type annotations (e.g., `def func(x: "SomeClass") -> "AnotherClass":`) for all type references, including those involving cyclic dependencies, and configure mypy with `--strict-optional`, `--warn-redundant-casts`, and `--warn-unused-configs` to ensure robust static type checking. Employ `typing.TYPE_CHECKING` guards to conditionally import types only during type checking, avoiding runtime import cycles. For sphinx-autodoc-typehints, enable the `autodoc_typehints = "description"` and `autodoc_typehints_description_target = "documented"` options to generate clean, readable documentation that includes type hints without causing parse errors due to cyclic references. Define all types in a single module or logical group of modules to minimize cross-module dependencies, and use `@typing.overload` where necessary to express function overloading behavior. Avoid circular imports in the runtime code path by ensuring that cyclic type dependencies are resolved via forward references and that no actual import of the dependent type occurs at runtime. This approach ensures full compatibility with mypy’s static analysis, pytest’s runtime execution, and sphinx-autodoc-typehints’ documentation generation, while supporting both recursive type definitions and full type expressiveness.

## Decision

Implement OpenShift's built-in Identity Provider (IdP) integration using OpenID Connect (OIDC) as the unified authentication and identity management solution across all applications deployed on Operate First. All applications will leverage OpenShift’s OAuth2-based authentication system, with user identity and session management centralized through OpenShift's authentication layer. This approach ensures that user credentials are managed consistently and securely within the OpenShift cluster, enabling Single Sign-On (SSO) across all applications without requiring individual user stores. The unique username, derived from the OpenShift IdP (e.g., from an external identity provider such as Keycloak, GitHub, or LDAP), will be used uniformly across all applications for RBAC enforcement, quota management, sandboxing, and audit logging. Application-level authorization will be based on OpenShift’s Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), with scopes and claims mapped from the OIDC identity token. This architecture eliminates identity silos, reduces operational overhead, ensures compliance with security best practices, and leverages the robust, battle-tested authentication infrastructure already provided by OpenShift. The solution is extensible, supports multi-identity provider backends, and aligns with the Operate First principle of using open, standardized, and cloud-native components.

## Decision: Introduce DynamoDB data access patterns into the benchmark to simulate real-world Lambda workloads.

To increase the realism and relevance of the benchmark, we will incorporate synthetic DynamoDB read and write operations that mirror common patterns observed in production Lambda functions. Each benchmark execution will include a configurable number of DynamoDB requests (e.g., GetItem, PutItem, Query, Scan) with realistic payload sizes and response latencies. The data access will be performed using the AWS SDK for JavaScript (Node.js) in a synchronous, non-pipelined manner, consistent with typical Lambda usage. We will simulate varying data access patterns—such as single-item reads with high-frequency access, batch operations, and conditional writes—to reflect diverse real-world use cases. The DynamoDB endpoints will be accessed via AWS Lambda’s built-in VPC endpoint or public internet, depending on the test configuration, to evaluate cold start and runtime performance under different network conditions. We will also include realistic error handling and retry logic (up to three retries with exponential backoff) to reflect actual application behavior. The benchmark will track metrics such as average latency per DynamoDB operation, total execution time, memory utilization during I/O, and error rates. This approach ensures the benchmark reflects not just computational work, but also the I/O and networking characteristics typical of real-world serverless applications, enabling more accurate performance comparisons across different runtime versions, memory configurations, and deployment strategies.

## Decision

The reference implementation shall preserve unrecognized fields in metadata files during deserialization and serialization, ensuring that such fields are not silently dropped or modified when the metadata is written back to disk. This behavior is required to maintain backward compatibility and support future extensibility as defined by TAPs 6, 10, 14, 15, and 16. The implementation must deserialize metadata into a generic, extensible data structure (e.g., a map or dictionary) that retains all top-level fields, regardless of recognition, and serialize them back in their original form, including unrecognized fields, without reordering or altering their values. This preserves the integrity of metadata across versions and enables future-proofing of the specification. The preservation of unrecognized fields is not subject to validation or filtering unless explicitly defined by a TAP. This decision ensures that metadata files can be safely passed between clients of different versions, with newer clients introducing new fields that older clients will ignore without causing validation errors or unintended modifications.

## Decision

We will select Microsoft Azure as our primary cloud provider for the development of the services. This decision is based on the following critical factors:

1. **EU Data Sovereignty**: Azure provides explicit guarantees that data remains within the European Union, both at rest and in transit, through its EU-only data residency commitments and compliance with GDPR. This is a non-negotiable requirement for our operations.

2. **Geo-Replicated Multi-Master Database**: Azure Cosmos DB offers globally distributed, horizontally scalable, multi-master databases with strong consistency, automatic sharding, and regional failover—all natively supported and fully managed. This capability is not available in AWS, and while Google Cloud Spanner offers similar features, it does not provide EU-only data residency.

3. **Comprehensive PaaS Ecosystem**: Azure delivers all required PaaS components—serverless functions (Azure Functions), event-driven messaging (Azure Service Bus and Event Hubs), push notifications (Azure Notification Hubs), email and SMS delivery (via integration with Sendgrid or Twilio), and centralized logging and telemetry (Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, Application Insights)—all with strong support for multi-region deployment and EU data isolation.

4. **Competitive TCO and Scalability**: Azure’s pricing model, combined with its auto-scaling and pay-per-use features, delivers competitive total cost of ownership while ensuring elastic scalability and 99.99% availability SLAs across all services.

5. **Compliance and Trust**: Azure’s extensive compliance certifications (including ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA) and its proven track record in regulated European markets further strengthen its suitability for our use case.

While Google Cloud and AWS offer strong alternatives, only Azure meets all the technical, compliance, and sovereignty requirements—especially the EU data residency guarantee and the availability of a fully managed, multi-master, globally distributed database. Therefore, Azure is the optimal choice for building a resilient, scalable, and sovereign cloud-native platform.

## Decision: Deprecate unused PostgreSQL configuration and remove database dependencies from production environments.

Given that PostgreSQL is configured in all environments but not actively used in production, we will deprecate the database configuration and remove all database dependencies from the production stack. This decision is based on the observed lack of database utilization, which indicates that the application does not require persistent relational storage in its current state. To reduce operational complexity, security surface area, and infrastructure costs, we will refactor the application to operate in a stateless, in-memory mode in production. Any data that was previously intended for PostgreSQL will be migrated to alternative persistent storage solutions—such as file-based storage, key-value stores, or cloud object storage—if retention is required. The configuration files will be updated to reflect the removal of PostgreSQL dependencies, and automated deployment pipelines will be adjusted to skip database initialization and connection steps. This change will be accompanied by a comprehensive audit of data flow and state management to ensure no data loss or functional regression occurs. The decision supports a leaner, more maintainable production environment aligned with actual usage patterns, while preserving the ability to reintroduce database functionality through a formal architectural review if future requirements demand it.

## Decision

The output directory structure for single-client generation should be simplified to `<outputDir>/serviceDir` instead of the current nested `<outputDir>/serviceDir/serviceDir` when generating from a single spec. This change aligns with the expected behavior of the `generate-X-client` command, which implies a single client output. The nested structure introduces unnecessary complexity and confusion, especially in manual usage scenarios where users expect a flat, predictable hierarchy. By flattening the output to `<outputDir>/serviceDir`, the generated files are placed directly under the service directory, reducing cognitive overhead and improving usability. This decision preserves backward compatibility for multi-client generation by maintaining the nested structure in that case, but defaults to the simplified form when only one spec is processed. The change is consistent with user expectations, reduces friction in common workflows, and enhances clarity without compromising functionality.

## Decision: Adopt a NoSQL database (specifically Azure Cosmos DB with SQL API) for persistent state storage in favor of Azure SQL, due to lower operational cost, improved scalability for non-relational data patterns, and sufficient support for query capabilities and consistency models required by the application. The decision is based on the system’s relatively simple data model, low transaction complexity, and minimal need for ACID transactions or complex joins. Cosmos DB offers serverless pricing tiers, global distribution, and predictable low-latency performance, aligning well with cost-sensitive and scalable requirements. While the relational model of Azure SQL provides strong consistency and advanced querying, the application’s data structure—predominantly document-based with hierarchical and semi-structured data—lends itself naturally to a NoSQL approach. The SQL API in Cosmos DB enables familiar querying syntax while maintaining the flexibility and performance benefits of a NoSQL backend. This choice reduces infrastructure costs, simplifies schema evolution, and supports future growth without over-provisioning. Additionally, Cosmos DB’s built-in support for automatic indexing, partitioning, and multi-region failover reduces operational overhead compared to managing Azure SQL manually. The trade-off in reduced relational integrity is mitigated by application-level constraints and data validation, which are feasible given the system’s simplicity. Overall, the shift to NoSQL provides a more cost-effective, scalable, and maintainable persistence solution that meets current and foreseeable future needs.

## Decision

We will decouple the deployment of essential platform applications (paas-admin, paas-billing, paas-accounts) from the main paas-cf deployment pipeline by treating them as independently versioned and deployable components. These applications will be built and deployed via their own dedicated CI/CD pipelines, with versioned releases published to a private registry.
